question: What is BERT?
answer: BERT stands for Bit Error Rate Test. Youll often hear BERT test, although this is technically redundant because the T in BERT stands for test. Still, saying, Were going to run some BERTs on the T1 will make everyone look at you funny. BERT tests are disruptive tests run on a link to validate the data integrity of the circuit. You usually run a BERT test by putting the remote end of the link in loop- back and sending out a special pattern of ones and zeros. How the data is returned from the far-e

question: What is Central Office (CO)?
answer: The central office is where phone lines from residences or businesses physically terminate. COs have the necessary switching equipment to route calls locally or to another carrier as needed. When you make a call that is destined for somewhere other than your premises, the CO is the first stop. With technology like T1, the copper connection from your location will probably terminate at a CO, where it may be aggregated into part of a larger SONET system.

question: What is Channel bank?
answer: A channel bank is a device that separates a T1 into 24 individual analog phone lines, and vice versa. Today, private branch exchanges (PBXs) usually take care of partitioning T1s into analog lines, thereby eliminating the need for a channel bank.

question: What is CSU/DSU?
answer: CSU stands for Channel Service Unit, and DSU stands for Data Service Unit. A CSU is responsible for interfacing with the WAN link, and a DSU is responsible for interfacing with data equipment such as routers. A CSU/DSU combines these functions into a single unit. Typically, an RJ-45-terminated cable will connect the demarc to the CSU/DSU, and a V.35 cable will connect the CSU/DSU to a router. The CSU/DSU is usually configurable to support all the common T1 signaling and framing options. Modern C

question: What is CPE?
answer: CPE is short for customer premises equipment (i.e., equipment that is located at the customers premises). Examples include a PBX, phones, routers, and even cable modems. Traditionally, the term was used to describe equipment owned by a tel- ephone service provider that resided at customer premises, but it has evolved to include equipment owned by anyone. Telecom engineers often shorten the word premises to prem when speaking.

question: What is DACCS?
answer: DACCS (pronounced dacks) stands for Digital Access Cross-Connect System. You may also see this as DAX, or DACS®, which is a registered trademark of AT&T. A DACCS is a device that allows changes to the way voice channels are connected between trunks, through the use of software. Figure 20-3 shows a logical representation of a DACCS in use. T1-A connects to the DACCS, and has 18 of its 24 channels in use. Those channels need to be routed to three different places. With the DACCS, we can link the f

question: What is Demarc?
answer: Demarc (pronounced dee-mark) is a slang abbreviation for demarcation point. The demarcation point is the point where the telecom providers responsibilities end and yours begin. Demarcs are often telecom closets or similar locations that can be secured to allow access for the telecom providers engineers. If you need your T1s to terminate somewhere in your building other than the demarc, the telecom provider may install an extended demark to accommodate your needs.

question: What is Digital signal hierarchy?
answer: The digital signal (DS) hierarchy describes the signaling rates of trunk links. These links are the physical links on which logical T-carriers are placed. The carrier numbers grow larger as the number of multiplexed DS0s increases. DS0 is the smallest designation, and is the rate required for a single phone line. The hierarchy is shown in Table 20-1. question: What is ISDN?
answer: ISDN stands for Integrated Services Digital Network. ISDN is a form of digital transmission for voice and data. Unlike normal POTS lines or channelized T1 serviceswhich use the voice path for signalingISDN uses a separate channel called the data channel for signaling, so the remaining channels (called bearer channels) can be used exclusively for voice. Because a separate channel is used for signaling, greater functionality is possible with ISDN. The bearer channels are sometimes referred to as B

question: What is BRI?
answer: BRI is short for Basic Rate Interface. A BRI is an ISDN link composed of two 64 Kbps bearer channels and one 16 Kbps data channel.

question: What is PRI?
answer: PRI is short for Primary Rate Interface. A PRI is an ISDN T1 link composed of twenty-three 64 Kbps bearer channels, and one 64 Kbps data channel. PRIs are used a lot for connecting PBX systems, or at ISPs for dial-up lines. While PRI circuits are used today for voice, BRI circuits, which were commonly used for data, have been widely replaced by cheaper alternatives such as DSL.

question: What is IXC?
answer: IXC stands for interexchange carrier. An IXC is a telephone company that supplies connections between local exchanges provided by local exchange carriers. Con- necting between LATAs may involve IXCs.

question: What is J-carrier?
answer: The J-carrier hierarchy is much closer to the US T-carrier hierarchy (in terms of speed) than the European hierarchy, though the values change as the rates get faster. question: What is LATA?
answer: LATA (pronounced lat-ah) is short for local access and transport area. LATAs are geographically defined areas in which a telecom provider can provide local service. The Regional Bell Operating Companies (RBOCs), for example, were usually not permitted to provide services between LATAs (interLATA), but could provide services within a LATA (intraLATA). LATAs come into play when point-to-point circuits like T1s are ordered. When a T1 starts and ends within the same LATA, the cost for the circuit is

question: What is Latency?
answer: Latency is the term used to describe the amount of time it takes for data to be processed or moved. Latency has nothing to do with the throughput, bandwidth, or speed of a link. Latency has to do with distance, the speed of light, and the amount of time it takes for hardware to process data. Latency on networks links is a combination of propagation delay and processing delay:

answer: Figure 20-4 shows three locations: New York, Cleveland, and Los Angeles. There are two links: one T1 between New York and Cleveland, and one T1 between New York and Los Angeles. Both links have the same speed (1.54 Mbps), but it takes longer for packets to get from New York to Los Angeles than it does for them to get from New York to Cleveland. The discrepancy occurs because Los Angeles is a lot farther away from New York than Cleveland is. This form of latency is called propagation delay. Prop-

question: What is LEC?
answer: LEC (pronounced leck) is short for local exchange carrier. A LEC is a phone com- pany that provides local service, as opposed to an IXC, which interconnects LECs to provide long-distance service. Most of the largest LECs are RBOCs.

question: What is Local loop?
answer: The local loop (also referred to as the last mile) is the copper handoff for a circuit from the telecom facility to your facility. While a T1 may be converted and multi- plexed into a larger circuit like a DS3 or SONET circuit, the last mile is usually copper.

question: What is Multiplexing?
answer: Multiplexing is the act of taking multiple signals and sharing them on a single signal. The act of converting twenty-four 64 Kbps channels into a single T1 is an example of multiplexing.

question: What is PBX?
answer: PBX is the abbreviation for private branch exchange. A PBX is essentially a phone system as most people know it; it offers a phone network to an entity such as an enterprise. Some of the main features of a PBX are the ability for many phones to share a limited number of public phone lines, and the ability to number individual extensions with, typically, three- or four-digit extension numbers. PBX systems have traditionally been large hardware devices with cryptic control systems and proprietary

question: What is POTS?
answer: POTS is short for the clever phrase plain-old telephone service. A POTS line is one into which you can plug in a normal analog phone or fax machine. Most home phone lines are POTS lines.

question: What is RBOC?
answer: RBOC (pronounced are-bock) is short for Regional Bell Operating Company. In 1875, Alexander Graham Bell (and two others who agreed to finance his inven- tions) started the Bell Telephone Company. Bell Telephone later became known as the Bell System as it acquired controlling interests in other companies such as Western Electric. In 1885, American Telephone and Telegraph (AT&T) was in- corporated to build and operate the USs original long-distance telephone network. In 1899, AT&T acquired Bell. F

question: What is Bell Atlantic?
answer: Bell Atlantic merged with NYNEX in 1996 to become Verizon.

question: What is Southwestern Bell?
answer: Southwestern Bell changed its name to SBC in 1995. SBC acquired PacBell in 1996, and has subsequently acquired Ameritech, Southern New England Tel- ecommunications, and AT&T. SBC adopted the name AT&T following the acquisition of that company.

question: What is NYNEX?
answer: NYNEX merged with Bell Atlantic in 1996 to become Verizon.

question: What is Pacific Bell (PacBell)?
answer: PacBell was acquired by SBC in 1996.

question: What is BellSouth?
answer: BellSouth has been acquired by SBC/AT&T.

question: What is Ameritech?
answer: Ameritech was acquired by SBC in 1998.

question: What is US West?
answer: US West was acquired by Qwest Communications in 2000.

question: What is Smart jack?
answer: A smart jack is a device that terminates a digital circuit. It is considered smart because the phone company can control it remotely. Smart jacks also offer test points for equipment such as BERT testers. T1s are usually terminated at smart jacks. Larger installations have racks of smart jacks called smart jack racks.

question: What is SONET?
answer: SONET (pronounced like bonnet) is short for synchronous optical network. SONET is an ANSI standard for fiber-optic transmission systems. The equivalent European standard is called the synchronous digital hierarchy (SDH). SONET is strictly optical, as its name suggests, and is very fast. SONET defines certain optical carrier levels, as shown in Table 20-4.

question: What is T-carrier?
answer: T-carrier is the generic name for digital multiplexed carrier systems. The letter T stands for trunk, as these links were originally designed to trunk multiple phone lines between central offices. The T-carrier hierarchy is used in the US and Canada. question: What is T-Berd?
answer: A T-Berd is a T1 Bit Error Rate Detector. The generic term is used for any device that will perform BERT tests on a T1. If you have a T1 thats misbehaving, the provider will probably send out an engineer with a T-Berd to perform invasive testing.

question: What is TDM?
answer: TDM stands for time-division multiplexing. A T1 link is a TDM link because its 24 channels are divided into time slots. A T1 link is a serial link, so one bit is sent at a time. The channels are cycled through at a high rate of speed, with each channel being dedicated to a slice of time.

question: What is Understanding T1 Duplex?
answer: A full-duplex link can send and receive data at the same time. As anyone whos ever had a fight with his or her significant other over the phone can attest, both parties on a call can talk (or scream) at the same time. This is a full-duplex conversation. If only one person could talk at a time, the conversation would be half duplex. Using walkie- talkies, where you have to push a button to talk, is an example of a half-duplex con- versation. question: What is (CSMA/CD)?
answer: A media-access mechanism that requires a node wishing to transmit to listen for a carrier signal before trying to send. If a carrier is sensed, the node waits for the transmission in progress to finish before initiating its own transmission. If a collision occurs and is detected, the sending node uses the backoff algorithm before retransmitting.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is (DHCP)?
answer: A protocol used to dynamically assign IP configurations to hosts. The services defined by the protocol are used to request and assign an IP address, a default gateway, and a DNS server address to a network host.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is (ISO)?
answer: An international standards body that defines many networking standards and that created the OSI model. International Telecommunications Union (ITU) A United Nations (UN) agency responsible for issues that concern information and communication technologies.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is AND (logical)?
answer: One of three basic binary logic operations. ANDing yields the following results: 1 AND 1 = 1, 1 AND 0 = 0, 0 AND 1 = 0, 0 AND 0 = 0. Key Terms Glossary

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is ARP cache?
answer: Logical storage in a host’s RAM for ARP entries. See also ARP table.

question: What is ARP table?
answer: Logical storage in a host’s RAM for ARP entries. See also ARP cache.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)?
answer: An internet protocol used to map an IP address to a MAC address. Defined in RFC 826.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Binary?
answer: Number expressed using the base-2 number system.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15)?
answer: A wireless personal area network (WPAN) standard that uses a device pairing process to communicate over distances from 1 to 100 meters.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP)?
answer: A protocol used by a network node to determine the IP address of its Ethernet interfaces in order to facilitate network booting.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is CSMA/Collision Detect (CSMA/CD)?
answer: See Carrier Sense Multiple Access/Collision Detect (CSMA/CD).

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is DMZ (demilitarized zone)?
answer: An area of an internal network where resources are available to the internet, such as a web server, and where devices have IPv6 addresses and public IPv4 addresses accessible through the internet.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Digital Subscriber Line (DSL)?
answer: An always-on internet service that provides high bandwidth and high availability. Voice and data signals are carried on different frequencies on the copper telephone wires. In general, small office and home office users connect using Asymmetrical DSL (ADSL), which means that the download speed is faster than the upload speed.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is File Transfer Protocol (FTP)?
answer: An application protocol that is part of the TCP/IP protocol stack and that is used for transferring files between network nodes. FTP is defined in RFC 959.

topic: Key Term: File Transfer Protocol Secure (FTPS)
source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is File Transfer Protocol Secure (FTPS)?
answer: An encrypted version of FTP.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Forwarding Information Base (FIB)?
answer: A data structure that contains all the known routes. Conceptually, the FIB is similar to a routing table. A networking device uses the FIB lookup table to make destination-based switching decisions.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)?
answer: A protocol that provides a set of rules for exchanging text, graphic images, sound, video, and other multimedia files on the World Wide Web. HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is IPv4 address?
answer: A 32-bit number, written in dotted decimal notation, used by the IPv4 protocol to uniquely identify an interface connected to an IP network. It is also used as a destination address in an IP header to allow routing. As a source address, it enables a computer to receive a packet and to know to which IP address a response should be sent.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is IPv6 address?
answer: A 126-bit address written in hexadecimal used by the IPv6 protocol. IPv6 addresses are the successor of IPv4 addresses. J–K–L

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Interchange (ASCII)?
answer: An 8-bit code (7 bits plus parity) for character representation.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is LTE?
answer: A designation for a 4G technology that meets the 4G speed standards.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Logical Link Control (LLC)?
answer: The IEEE 802.2 standard that defines the upper sublayer of the Ethernet Layer 2 specifications (and other LAN standards).

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is MAC address table?
answer: On a switch, a table that lists all known MAC addresses and the bridge/switch port that should be used to forward frames sent to each MAC address.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Neighbor Advertisement message?
answer: An ICMPv6 message sent by a device in response to an ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation message; it contains the IPv6 address and the corresponding MAC address.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Neighbor Discovery (ND)?
answer: A protocol that provides address resolution, router discovery, and redirection services for IPv6 using ICMPv6.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Neighbor Solicitation message?
answer: An ICMPv6 message sent by a device when it knows the IPv6 address but needs the corresponding MAC address.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is NetBIOS (NetBT)?
answer: A system through which older computer applications can communicate over large TCP/IP networks.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe)?
answer: A specification that was developed specifically to allow computers to take greater advantage of the features of SSDs by providing a standard interface between SSDs, the PCIe bus, and operating systems.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is POP3?
answer: See Post Office Protocol 3 (POP3).

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Post Office Protocol (POP)?
answer: A protocol that allows a computer to retrieve email from a server.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Post Office Protocol 3 (POP3)?
answer: A protocol used by email clients to retrieve messages from an email server.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Protocol)?
answer: A protocol that enables network administrators to monitor network operations from centralized monitoring stations.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is RJ-11 connector?
answer: A physical network interface used to connect a computer to a standard telephone line.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is RJ-45 connector?
answer: A standardized physical network interface for connecting telecommunications or data equipment. The most common twisted-pair connector is an 8-position, 8-contact (8P8C) modular plug and jack.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is ROM?
answer: See read-only memory (ROM).

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Regional Internet Registry (RIR)?
answer: One of the five organizations responsible for allocating IP addresses within particular geographic regions.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Request for Comments (RFC)?
answer: A series of documents and memoranda encompassing new protocols, research, innovations, and methodologies applicable to internet technologies. RFCs are developed by the IETF for the TCP/IP protocol suite.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Router Advertisement (RA) message?
answer: An ICMPv6 message sent by a router to provide addressing information to hosts using SLAAC.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Router Solicitation message?
answer: An ICMPv6 message sent by devices to request an ICMPv6 Router Advertisement message.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is SLAAC?
answer: See stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC).

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is SMB/CIFS?
answer: Protocols that allow for sharing of files, printers, and other resources between nodes on a network. CIFS is a dialect of SMB. SNMP (Simple Network Management

topic: Key Term: SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP)
source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP)?
answer: An extension to Secure Shell (SSH) protocol that can be used to establish a secure file transfer session.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Secure Shell (SSH)?
answer: A protocol that provides a secure remote connection to a host through a TCP application.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Secure)?
answer: A set of rules for exchanging text, graphic images, sound, and video on the World Wide Web. HTTPS adds encryption and authentication services using Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) protocol or the newer Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Server Message Block (SMB)?
answer: An application level network protocol mainly applied to shared

topic: Key Term: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)
source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)?
answer: An application layer protocol that provides electronic mail services to transfer mail from client to server and between servers.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Solicitation (RS) message?
answer: See Router Solicitation message.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is TCP/IP model?
answer: A conceptual framework that consists of layers that perform functions necessary to prepare data for transmission over a network. Telecommunications Industry Association/ Electronic Industries Association (TIA/EIA) An organization that develops standards that relate to telecommunications technologies. Together, the TIA and the Electronic Industries Alliance (EIA) have formalized standards, such as EIA/TIA-232, for the electrical characteristics of data transmission.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Time-to-Live (TTL)?
answer: A field in the IP header that prevents a packet from indefinitely looping around an IP internetwork. A router decrements the TTL field each time it forwards a packet, and if it decrements the TTL to 0, the router discards the packet, which prevents it from looping forever.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)?
answer: A Layer 4 protocol of the TCP/IP model that lets applications guarantee delivery of data across a network.

topic: Key Term: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP)
source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP)?
answer: A protocol similar to FTP that enables the transfer of

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Trojan horse?
answer: A type of malware named after the wooden horse the Greeks used to infiltrate Troy. It is a harmful piece of software that looks legitimate. Users are typically tricked into loading and executing Trojans on their systems.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11)?
answer: A wireless LAN (WLAN) technology that uses a contention-based protocol known as CSMA/CA. The wireless NIC must first listen before transmitting to determine if the radio channel is clear. If another wireless device is transmitting, the NIC must wait until the channel is clear. Wi-Fi, which is a trademark of the Wi-Fi Alliance, is used with certified WLAN devices based on the IEEE 802.11 standards.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is Wi-Fi analyzer?
answer: A mobile tool for auditing and troubleshooting wireless networks.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is WiMAX (IEEE 802:16)?
answer: Worldwide Interoperability for Microware Access, a wireless standard that uses a point-to-multipoint topology to provide wireless broadband access.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is access attack?
answer: A type of attack that exploits known vulnerabilities in authentication services, FTP services, and web services to gain entry to web accounts, confidential databases, and other sensitive information. An access attack allows individuals to gain unauthorized access to information that they have no right to view.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is access method?
answer: A set of rules used by LAN hardware to direct traffic on the network. It determines which host or device uses the LAN next.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is access point (AP)?
answer: A device that connects to a wireless router and is used to extend the reach of a wireless network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is accounting)?
answer: The primary framework to set up access control on a network device.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is acknowledgment?
answer: A notification sent from one network device to another to acknowledge that some event (for example, receipt of a message) has occurred.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is adjacency table?
answer: A table in a router that contains a list of the relationships formed between selected neighboring routers and end nodes for the purpose of exchanging routing information. Adjacency is based on the use of a common media segment.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is alternating current?
answer: An electrical current that changes direction at a uniformly repetitious rate. This type of electricity typically is provided by a utility company and is accessed through wall sockets. American National Standards Institute (ANSI) A private nonprofit organization that oversees development of standards in the United States. American Standard Code for Information

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is analog telephone?
answer: A type of telephone that can transmit data over standard voice telephone lines for internet access. This type of service uses an analog modem to place a telephone call to another modem at a remote site. This method of connection is known as dialup.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is ance (CSMA/CA)?
answer: A media-access mechanism that regulates the transmission of data onto a network medium. CSMA/CA is similar to CSMA/CD except that devices first request the right to send, in order to avoid collisions. CSMA/CA is used in 802.11 WLANs. Carrier Sense Multiple Access/Collision Detect

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is assigned multicast?
answer: Reserved IPv6 multicast addresses for predefined groups of devices.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is asymmetric switching?
answer: A switching technique that allows for different data rates on different ports. authentication, authorization, and accounting See AAA (authentication, authorization, and accounting). automatic medium-dependent interface cross-

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is availability?
answer: The assurance of timely and reliable access to data services for authorized users. Network firewall devices, along with desktop and server antivirus software, can ensure system reliability and the robustness to detect, repel, and cope with breaches of network security. Building fully redundant network infrastructures, with few single points of failure, can reduce the impact of these threats.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is baby giant frame?
answer: An Ethernet frame with more than 1500 bytes of data. Also known as a jumbo frame.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is bandwidth?
answer: The rated throughput capacity of a given network medium or protocol. Bandwidth is listed as available or consumed data communication resources expressed in bits per second.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is best effort?
answer: Describes the agreement or the attempt to fulfill expectations or the requirements of a standard.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is best-effort delivery?
answer: Describes a network system that does not use a sophisticated acknowledgment system to guarantee reliable delivery of information.

topic: Key Term: bring your own device (BYOD)
source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is bring your own device (BYOD)?
answer: A policy that allows end users to use personal tools to access information and communicate across a business or campus network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is broadcast?
answer: A form of transmission in which one device transmits to all devices within the network or on another network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is broadcast address?
answer: A special address reserved for sending a message to all stations. Generally, a broadcast address is a MAC destination address of all ones. Compare with multicast address and unicast address.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is brute-force attack?
answer: An attempt to access usernames or passwords by trial and error.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is buffered memory?
answer: A memory chip that has a control chip built into the module. The control chip assists the memory controller in managing large quantities of RAM.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is burned-in address (BIA)?
answer: The MAC address that is permanently assigned to a LAN interface or NIC. It is called burned-in because the address is burned into a chip on the card, and the address cannot be changed. Also called universally administered address (UAA).

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is bus topology?
answer: A network topology in which all end systems are chained to each other and terminated in some form on each end. Infrastructure devices such as switches are not required to interconnect the end devices. Legacy Ethernet networks were often bus topologies using coax cables because it was inexpensive and easy to set up.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is cable connection?
answer: The point at which a cable connects to the device.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is cable internet?
answer: A form of internet service that uses coaxial cable lines originally designed to carry cable television and connects an end user’s computer to the cable company.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is cable tester?
answer: A testing device used to check for wiring shorts, faults, or wires connected to the wrong pins. Carrier Sense Multiple Access (CSMA) A media-access mechanism in which devices ready to transmit data first check the channel for a carrier. If no carrier is sensed for a specific period of time, a device can transmit. See also CSMA/CA and CSMA/CD.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is cellular connection?
answer: Cellular internet access that uses a cell phone network to connect. Wherever a user can get a cellular signal, the user can get cellular internet access. Performance is limited by the capabilities of the phone and the cell tower to which it is connected.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is channel?
answer: A communication path over a medium used to transport information from a sender to a receiver. Multiple channels can be multiplexed over a single cable.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is circuit switched?
answer: A switching system in which a dedicated physical circuit path exists between sender and receiver for the duration of the call. Used heavily in the telephone company network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is classful addressing?
answer: A type of addressing in which a unicast IP address has three parts: a network part, a subnet part, and a host part. The term classful refers to the fact that the classful network rules are first applied to the address, and then the rest of the address can be separated into a subnet and host part to perform subnetting. Originally, IPv4 addresses were divided into five classes: Class A, Class B, Class C, Class D, and Class E. Classful addressing is not generally practiced in current network implementations.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is classless addressing?
answer: An IPv4 addressing scheme that uses a subnet mask that does not follow classful addressing limitations. It provides increased flexibility when dividing ranges of IP addresses into separate networks. Classless addressing is considered the best in current network implementations. See also variable length subnet masking (VLSM).

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is client?
answer: A network device that accesses a service on another computer remotely through a network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is client/server?
answer: A computer system setup in which tasks are distributed between a service provider (server) and a service user, such as a workstation (client). The server is used to store the applications and data, and the majority of the computer processing is done on the server.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is cloud computing?
answer: Computing resources (hardware and software) delivered as a service over a network. A company uses the hardware and software in the cloud, and a service fee is charged.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is cloud storage?
answer: Online storage that is accessed via the internet.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is coaxial cable (coax)?
answer: Cable consisting of a hollow outer cylindrical conductor that surrounds a single inner wire conductor. Two types of coaxial cable are currently used in LANs: 50-ohm cable, which is used for digital signaling, and 75-ohm cable, which is used for analog signaling.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is collaboration?
answer: A process in which more than one person works on a document or documents in real time across a network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is collision fragment?
answer: Any frame less than 64 bytes in length. These frames are automatically discarded by receiving stations. Also called runt frame.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is command-line interface (CLI)?
answer: A user interface to a computer operating system or application that depends on textual commands being entered by the user.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is communication?
answer: Transmission and receipt of information.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is communities?
answer: Groups of people who share common experiences and hobbies and who exchange ideas and information. Communities allow for social interaction that is independent of location or time zone.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is confidentiality?
answer: The state of ensuring that only intended and authorized recipients—individuals, processes, or devices—can access and read data. Confidentiality is accomplished by having a strong system for user authentication, enforcing passwords that are difficult to guess, and requiring users to change passwords frequently. Encrypting data so that only the intended recipient can read it is also part of confidentiality. Cisco Internetwork Operating System (IOS) Generic term for the collection of network operating systems used by Cisco networking devices.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is congested?
answer: A condition in which a network has more bits to transmit than the bandwidth of the communication channel can deliver.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is congestion?
answer: Traffic in excess of network capacity.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is connection oriented?
answer: Term used to describe data transfer that requires the establishment of a virtual circuit.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is connection-oriented protocol?
answer: A protocol that requires the establishment of a virtual circuit.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is connectionless?
answer: Term used to describe data transfer without the existence of a virtual circuit.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is connectivity?
answer: The state of being connected or interconnected to another device.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is console?
answer: Term used to describe data transfer that requires the establishment of a virtual circuit. content addressable memory (CAM)

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is contention-based access method?
answer: A nondeterministic method of networking, which means any device can try to transmit data across the shared medium whenever it has data to send.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is converged data network?
answer: A network that aggregates various forms of traffic, such as voice, video, and data, on the same network infrastructure.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is core?
answer: The light transmission element at the center of optical fiber.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is crimper?
answer: A tool used to attach connectors to wires to make a cable.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is crosstalk?
answer: A source of interference that occurs when cables are bundled together for long lengths, in which the signal from one cable leaks out and enters adjacent cables. See also electromagnetic interference (EMI). CSMA/Collision Avoidance (CSMA/CA) See Carrier Sense Multiple Access/Collision Avoidance (CSMA/CA).

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is custom cloud?
answer: A cloud built to meet the needs of a specific industry, such as healthcare or media. Custom clouds can be private or public.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is cut-through switching?
answer: A frame forwarding method that forwards a frame before it is entirely received. At a minimum, the destination address of the frame must be read before the frame can be forwarded.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is cyclic redundancy check (CRC)?

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is daemon?
answer: A computer program that runs in the background and is usually initiated as a process. Daemons often support server processes.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is data center?
answer: A facility that houses computer systems and associated components, including redundant data communications connections, high-speed virtual servers, redundant storage systems, and security devices.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is data network?
answer: Infrastructure historically used by businesses to record and manage business systems. Data networks have evolved to enable the transmission of many different types of information services, including email, video, messaging, and telephony.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is datagram?
answer: A logical grouping of information sent as a network layer unit over a transmission medium without prior establishment of a virtual circuit. IP datagrams are the primary information units in the internet. Frames, messages, packets, and segments are also terms for datagrams. See also protocol data unit (PDU).

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is de-encapsulation?
answer: See decapsulation.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is decapsulation?
answer: A process by which an end device, after it receives data over some transmission medium, examines the headers and trailers at each successively higher layer, and eventually hands the data to the correct application. Sometimes called de-encapsulation.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is decoding?
answer: To convert from one form to another.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is default gateway?
answer: A device on a network that serves as an access point to other networks. A default gateway is used by a host to forward IP packets that have destination addresses outside the local subnet. A router interface typically is

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is default route?
answer: A route that needs zero (no) bits to match with the destination IP address of the packet.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is denial of service (DoS)?
answer: An attack that consumes system resources in order to prevent authorized people from using a service. To help prevent DoS attacks, it is important to stay up to date with the latest security updates for operating systems and applications.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is destination?
answer: The device that is the intended recipient of the message.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is destination port number?
answer: A UDP or TCP port number associated with the destination application on the remote device.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is dial-up telephone connection?
answer: An inexpensive communications option that uses any phone line and a modem. The low bandwidth provided by a dial-up modem connection is not sufficient for large data transfer, although it is useful for mobile access while traveling.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is digital camera?
answer: An input device that captures images and videos that can be stored, displayed, printed, or altered.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is directed broadcast?
answer: A term that describes IPv4 packets sent to all hosts in a particular network. In a directed broadcast, a single copy of the packet is routed to the specified network, where it is broadcast to all hosts on that network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is directly connected network?
answer: A network that is connected to a router’s physical Ethernet or serial interfaces.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is dotted decimal?
answer: The representation of an IPv4 address using four decimal numbers separated by periods.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is dual stack?
answer: A term for a device that is enabled for both IPv4 and IPv6 protocols.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is duplex?
answer: A setting used for communications on a network. See also half duplex and full duplex.

topic: Key Term: duplex multimode LC connector
source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is duplex multimode LC connector?
answer: A fiber connector that accepts both the transmitting and receiving fibers in a single connector. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is dynamic routing protocols?
answer: Protocols such as EIGRP and OSPF that are used to access remote networks.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is electromagnetic interference (EMI)?
answer: Interference by magnetic signals caused by the flow of electricity. EMI can cause reduced data integrity and increased error rates on transmission channels. Electrical currents create magnetic fields, which in turn cause other electrical currents in nearby wires, and the induced electrical currents can interfere with proper operation of the other wire.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is enable password?
answer: An unencrypted password used to limit access to privileged EXEC mode from IOS user EXEC mode.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is enable secret?
answer: An encrypted password used to limit access to privileged EXEC mode from IOS user EXEC mode.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is encapsulation?
answer: The process by which a device adds networking headers and trailers to data from an application for the eventual transmission of the data onto a transmission medium.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is encoding?
answer: A process by which bits are represented on a medium.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is end device?
answer: Either the source or destination of a message transmitted over a network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is expectational acknowledgment?
answer: An acknowledgment used by TCP where the ACK number is sent back to the source to indicate the next byte that the receiver expects to receive.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is extended star topology?
answer: A hierarchical star topology with devices connected to a central device and additional devices connected to those devices.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is extranet?
answer: Part of a network that provides secure and safe access to individuals who work for a different organization but require access to the organization’s data.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is fast-forward switching?
answer: A type of switching that offers a low level of latency by immediately forwarding a packet after reading the destination address.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is fault tolerant network?
answer: A term for limiting the impact of a failure so that the fewest number of devices are affected and for the shortest time.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is fiber optics?
answer: A technology that uses light to transmit data.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is fiber-optic cable?
answer: A physical medium that uses glass or plastic threads to transmit data. A fiberoptic cable consists of a bundle of these threads, each of which is capable of transmitting data into light waves.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is firewall?
answer: A hardware or software device that protects a computer or a network by preventing undesirable traffic from entering internal networks.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is firmware?
answer: Permanent software programmed into ROM memory.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is flow control?
answer: The management of data flow between devices in a network. It is used to prevent too much data from arriving before a device can handle it, causing data overflow.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is fragment-free switching?
answer: A type of switching in which a switch stores the first 64 bytes of

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is fragmentation?
answer: The division of IP datagrams to meet the MTU requirements of a Layer 2 protocol.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is full-duplex?
answer: Bidirectional communication in which both devices can transmit and receive on the media at the same time.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is gateway?
answer: Normally, a relatively general term that refers to different kinds of networking devices. Historically, when routers were created, they were called gateways.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is global configuration mode?
answer: A mode used to configure global parameters or enter other configuration submodes, such as interface, router, and line configuration submodes.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is global routing prefix?
answer: An IPv6 prefix, or network, portion of an address that is assigned by the provider, such as an ISP, to a customer or site.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is global unicast address (GUA)?
answer: An IPv6 address similar to a public IPv4 address. It is a globally unique, internet-routable address. Global unicast addresses can be configured statically or assigned dynamically.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is goodput?
answer: Application-level throughput. It is the number of useful bits per unit of time from a certain source address to a certain destination, excluding protocol overhead and excluding retransmitted data packets.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is graphical user interface (GUI)?
answer: A user-friendly interface that uses graphical images and widgets, along with text, to indicate the information and actions available to a user when interacting with a computer.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is half-duplex?
answer: Unidirectional communication in which devices can transmit and receive on the media but cannot do so simultaneously.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is hexadecimal (base 16)?
answer: A number system using the digits 0 through 9, with their usual meaning, plus the letters A through F to represent hexadecimal digits with values of 10 to 15. The rightmost digit counts ones, the next counts multiples of 16, and 162 = 256.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is hextet?
answer: The unofficial term used to refer to a segment of 16 bits or 4 hexadecimal values. For IPv6 addressing, each digit is a single hextet, 16 bits, or 4 hexadecimal digits.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is host address?
answer: The IPv4 address of a network host. A network layer address.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is hub?

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is hybrid cloud?
answer: A cloud made up of two or more clouds (for example, part custom, part public), where each part remains a distinctive object, but the two are connected using a single architecture.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is initial sequence number (ISN)?
answer: A randomly chosen number that is used to begin tracking the flow of data from the client to the server for a session. The ISN in the header of each segment is increased by one for each byte of data sent from the client to the server as the data conversation continues. Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is integrity?
answer: The assurance that information has not been altered in transmission from origin to destination. Data integrity can be compromised when information has been corrupted—willfully or accidentally. Data integrity is made possible by requiring validation of the sender as well as using mechanisms to validate that the packet has not changed during transmission.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is interface?
answer: A specialized port on a networking device that connects to individual networks. Because routers are used to interconnect networks, the ports on a router are referred to as network interfaces.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is interface ID?
answer: The host portion of an IPv6 global unicast address.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is intermediary device?
answer: A device that connects end devices to the network and can connect multiple individual networks to form an internetwork. International Organization for Standardization

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is internet?
answer: A network that combines enterprise networks, individual users, and ISPs into a single global IP network. Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) An organization that assigns the numbers important to the proper operation of TCP/IP and the internet, including assigning globally unique IP addresses. Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) A protocol that is part of the TCP/IP internet layer and that defines protocol messages used to inform network engineers of how well an internetwork is working. For example, the ping command sends ICMP messages to determine whether a host can send packets to another host. Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) A protocol that describes a method to retrieve email messages. Copies of the messages are downloaded to the client application, but the original messages are kept on the server until manually deleted.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is internet query?
answer: A query that searches the internet, including Google search, the websites of organizations, whois, and more.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is internet service provider (ISP)?
answer: A company that helps create the internet by providing connectivity to enterprises and individuals, as well as interconnecting to other ISPs to create connectivity to all other ISPs.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is intranet?
answer: A private connection of LANs and WANs that belongs to an organization and that is designed to be accessible only by the organization’s members, employees, or others with authorization.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is intrusion detection system (IDS)?
answer: A system that passively monitors traffic on a network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is intrusion prevention system (IPS)?
answer: A system that monitors incoming and outgoing traffic, looking for malware, network attack signatures, and more. If it recognizes a threat, it can immediately stop it.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is jacket?
answer: The outer part of a fiber-optical cable, which protects the cable from abrasion, moisture, and other contaminants.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is jumbo frame?
answer: An Ethernet frame with more than 1500 bytes of data. Also known as a baby giant frame.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is kernel?
answer: The portion of the operating system that interacts directly with computer hardware.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is latency?
answer: Refers to the amount of time, including delays, for data to travel from one given point to another. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) A protocol used to maintain user identity directory information that can be shared across networks and systems.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is limited broadcast?
answer: A broadcast that is sent to a specific network or series of networks.

topic: Key Term: line of sight wireless
source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is line of sight wireless?
answer: An always-on service that uses radio signals for transmitting data and internet access. A clear path between the transmission tower and customer is required.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is link-local IPv4 address?
answer: An IPv4 address in the range 169.254.1.0 to 169.254.254.255. Communication using such an address has a TTL of 1 and is limited to the local network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is link-local IPv6 address?
answer: An IPv6 address used to communicate with other devices on the same local link. With IPv6, the term link refers to a subnet. A link-local address is confined to a single link. Its uniqueness must only be confirmed on that link because it is not routable beyond the link.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is local-area network (LAN)?

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is logical address?
answer: An address that is used to send a packet from a source device to a destination device on the same network or a different network. Typically an IP address.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is logical topology diagram?
answer: A map of the devices on a network, representing how the devices communicate with each other. It identifies the devices, ports, and addressing scheme.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is loopback?
answer: A special reserved IPv4 address, 127.0.0.1, or IPv6 address, ::1, that can be used to test TCP/IP applications. Packets sent to 127.0.0.1 (or ::1) by a computer never leave the computer or even require a working NIC. Instead, the packet is processed by IP at the lowest layer and is then sent back up the TCP/IP stack to another application on that same computer.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is loopback adapter?
answer: A device that tests the basic functionality of computer ports. The adapter is specific to the port being tested.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is loopback interface?
answer: A virtual interface that can be used to connect or identify a device using an IP address.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is maximum transmission unit (MTU)?
answer: The largest IP packet size allowed to be sent out a particular interface. Ethernet interfaces default to an MTU of 1500 because the data field of a standard Ethernet frame should be limited to 1500 bytes, and the IP packet sits inside the Ethernet frame’s data field. The Gigabit Ethernet standard supports jumbo frames, which can be as large as 9216 bytes, including tagging.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is media independent?
answer: A term that describes the networking layers whose processes are not affected by the media being used. In Ethernet, these are all the layers from the LLC sublayer of the data link layer upward.

topic: Key Term: medium to large network
source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is medium to large network?
answer: A network used by a corporation or school that has many locations with hundreds or thousands of interconnected computers.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is metropolitan-area network (MAN)?
answer: A network that spans a large campus or a city.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is modem?
answer: A device that converts signals produced by one type of device to a form compatible with another device, often used to connect a home or small office to the internet.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is multicast?
answer: A message sent to selected hosts that are part of a group. A single packet is copied by the network and sent to a specific subset of network addresses. These addresses are specified

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is multimeter?
answer: A device that measures AC/DC voltage, electric current, and other electrical characteristics and that can be used to test the integrity of circuits and the quality of electricity in computer components.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is multimode fiber (MMF)?
answer: Optical fiber that consists of a larger core and uses LED emitters to send light pulses.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is multiplexing?
answer: A process in which multiple digital data streams are combined into one signal.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is network address?
answer: A dotted decimal number defined by IPv4 to represent a network or subnet. It represents the network in which hosts reside. Also called a network number or network ID.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is network architecture?
answer: A collection of technologies that support the infrastructure and the programmed services and rules, or protocols, that move data across a network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is network attached storage (NAS)?
answer: Servers that are connected to a network to provide file-level data storage to clients using a centralized storage location.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is network infrastructure?
answer: The architecture defining the connections within a network; refers to the physical hardware and connections used to transmit data.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is network interface card (NIC)?
answer: Computer hardware, typically used for LANs, that allows a computer to connect to some networking cable. The NIC can then send and receive data over the cable at the direction of the computer.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is next hop?
answer: The next gateway to which a Layer 3 packet is delivered in order to reach the destination.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is nibble boundary?

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is noise?
answer: Interference, such as EMI or RFI, that causes unclean power and may cause errors in a computer system.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is nonreturn to zero (NRZ)?
answer: A line code in which 1s are represented by one significant condition and 0s are represented by another.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is nonvolatile RAM (NVRAM)?
answer: RAM that does not lose its contents when the device is powered off.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is nonvolatile memory?
answer: Memory whose contents are not erased when the computer is powered off.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is nslookup?
answer: A service or a program used to look up information in Domain Name System (DNS).

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is octet?
answer: A group of 8 binary bits. It is similar to, but not the same as, a byte. One application in computer networking is to use octets to divide IPv4 addresses into four components.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is octet boundary?
answer: The part of an IPv4 address that falls between octets. organizationally unique identifier (OUI) The first half of a MAC address. Manufacturers must ensure that the value of the OUI has been registered with the IEEE. This value identifies the manufacturer of any Ethernet NIC or interface.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is output device?
answer: A hardware device that takes the data processed from input and passes on the information for use.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is over (auto-MDIX)?
answer: A feature on a switch port or hub port that detects the type of cable used between switches or hubs. Once the cable type is detected, the port is connected and configured accordingly. With auto-MDIX, a crossover cable or a straight-through cable can be used for connections to a copper 10/100/1000 port on the switch, regardless of the type of device on the other end of the connection.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is overhead?
answer: Resources used to manage or operate a network. Overhead consumes bandwidth and reduces the amount of application data that can be transported across the network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is packet switched?
answer: A network architecture that routes packets along the path perceived as the most efficient and allows a communications channel to be shared by multiple connections.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is parallel port?
answer: A port that has a 25-pin receptacle used to connect various peripheral devices.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is peer-to-peer (P2P)?
answer: A type of networking in which each device serves as both a client and a server portion of an application. P2P also describes a small local network where a host can play the role of a client and/or a server.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is peer-to-peer file sharing?
answer: A system that allows people to share files with each other without having to store and download them from a central server. The user joins a P2P network by simply installing the P2P software. P2P file sharing has not been embraced by everyone. Many people are concerned about violating the laws of copyrighted materials.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is personal-area network (PAN)?
answer: A network that connects devices, such as mice, keyboards, printers, smartphones, and tablets, within the range of an individual person.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is physical address?
answer: An address used for NICto-NIC communications on the same Ethernet network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is physical media?
answer: The cabling and connectors used to interconnect network devices.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is physical port?
answer: A connector or an outlet on a networking device where the media are connected to an end device or another networking device.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is physical topology?
answer: The arrangement of the nodes in a network and the physical connections between them. It provides a representation of how the media are used to connect the devices.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is physical topology diagram?
answer: A diagram that identifies the physical locations of intermediary devices and cable installation.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is ping?
answer: A troubleshooting tool used to verify network connectivity by sending a packet to a specific IP address and waiting for the reply.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is ping sweep?
answer: The process of systematically pinging all network addresses in a given range or subnet. This is similar to going through a section of a telephone book and calling each number to see who answers.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is port?
answer: (1) With Ethernet hub and switch hardware, another name for an interface, which is a physical connector in the switch into which a cable can be connected. (2) With TCP and UDP, a software function that uniquely identifies a software process on a computer that uses TCP or UDP. (3) With PCs, a physical connector on a PC, such as a parallel port or a USB port.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is port number?
answer: A TCP or UDP field used to identify the source or destination application.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is port scan?
answer: A method of determining what TCP or UDP ports are open or listening on a remote device.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is power over Ethernet (PoE)?
answer: The powering of network devices over Ethernet cable. PoE is defined by two different standards: IEEE 802.3af and Cisco.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is power-on self-test (POST)?
answer: The hardware check that the basic input/output system (BIOS) performs on the main components of a computer at boot.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is powerline networking?
answer: An emerging trend for home networking that uses existing electrical wiring to connect devices.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is preferred format?
answer: The IPv6 address format x:x:x:x:x:x:x:x, with each x consisting of four hexadecimal values.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is prefix length?
answer: In IP subnetting, the portion of a set of IP addresses whose values must be identical for the addresses to be in the same subnet.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is private address?
answer: As defined in RFC 1918, an IP address that does not have to be globally unique because the address exists inside packets only when the packets are inside a single private IP internetwork. Private IP addresses are popularly used in most companies today, with NAT translating the private IP addresses into globally unique IP addresses.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is private cloud?
answer: A repository of cloud-based applications and services intended for a specific organization or entity, such as the government.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is privileged executive (EXEC) mode?

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is protocol?
answer: A written specification that defines what tasks a service or device should perform. Each protocol defines messages, often in the form of headers, plus the rules and processes by which the messages are used to achieve some stated purpose.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is protocol analyzer?
answer: A network monitoring device that gathers information regarding the status of a network and devices attached to it. Also known as a network analyzer or packet sniffer.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is protocol data unit (PDU)?
answer: A generic term that refers to the data, headers, and trailers about which a particular networking layer is concerned.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is protocol suite?
answer: A delineation of networking protocols and standards into different categories, called layers, along with definitions of which sets of standards and protocols need to be implemented to create products that can be used to create a working network.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is proxy server?
answer: A computer system that has the authority to act as another computer to function as a relay between client and server.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is public address?
answer: An IP address that has been registered with IANA or one of its member agencies to guarantee that the address is globally unique. Globally unique public IP addresses can be used for packets sent through the internet.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is public cloud?
answer: Cloud-based applications and services made available to the general population. Q–R

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is quality of service (QoS)?
answer: A control mechanism that can provide different priorities to different users or data flows or guarantee a certain level of

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is queuing?
answer: In routing and switching, a backlog of packets or frames waiting to be forwarded out an interface.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is radio frequency interference (RFI)?
answer: Noise that interferes with information being transmitted across unshielded copper cabling.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is random-access memory (RAM)?
answer: Also known as read/write memory, memory that can have new data written to it and that can have stored data read from it. RAM is the main working area, or temporary storage, used by a CPU for most processing and operations. A drawback of RAM is that it requires electrical power to maintain data storage. If the computer is turned off or loses power, all data stored in RAM is lost unless the data was previously saved to disk. Memory boards with RAM chips plug into the motherboard.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is read-only memory (ROM)?
answer: Nonvolatile memory located on the motherboard and other circuit boards that contain instructions that can be directly accessed by a CPU.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is real-time traffic?
answer: Data traffic that carries signal output as it happens or as fast as possible. Realtime traffic is sensitive to latency and jitter.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is reconnaissance attack?
answer: An attack that is used to discover and map systems, services, or vulnerabilities.

source: Introduction to Networks Companion Guide (CCNAv7) - Glossary
question: What is redundancy?
