What are the three modes of the vi/vim editor?
answer: 1. COMMAND MODE (default on open): keys execute commands (move, delete, copy). Press Esc to return here. 2. INSERT MODE: type text. Enter with i (insert before cursor), a (append after), o (open new line). 3. EX/LINE MODE: enter commands with : (colon) — :w (save), :q (quit), :wq (save & quit), :q! (quit without saving).

question: What are the vi movement keys?
answer: h (left), j (down), k (up), l (right). Word movement: w (next word), b (back word), e (end of word). Line movement: 0 (start of line), $ (end of line). File movement: G (go to last line), gg (go to first line), Ctrl+F (page down), Ctrl+B (page up).

question: What are common uses of the find command?
answer: find [path] [expression]. By name: find /etc -name '*.conf'. By size: find / -size +100M. By user: find /home -user bob. By permission: find / -perm 644. By time: find / -mtime -7 (modified last 7 days). Execute: find /tmp -name '*.tmp' -exec rm {} \; (use -ok for confirmation).

question: What are common Linux process signals and their uses?
answer: SIGNAL 1 (SIGHUP): reload configuration. SIGNAL 2 (SIGINT): interrupt (Ctrl+C). SIGNAL 9 (SIGKILL): force kill (cannot be caught). SIGNAL 15 (SIGTERM): terminate gracefully (default). SIGNAL 18 (SIGCONT): continue stopped process. SIGNAL 19 (SIGSTOP): stop process (cannot be caught). kill -9 PID to force kill. killall -9 NAME to kill by name. pkill for pattern-based killing.

topic: Linux Bible Ch10: dnf package management
question: What are the essential dnf commands for package management?
answer: dnf search <keyword> — search packages. dnf install <pkg> — install. dnf remove <pkg> — remove. dnf update — update all. dnf update <pkg> — update specific. dnf info <pkg> — show info. dnf list installed — list installed. dnf groupinstall '<group>' — install group. dnf provides <file> — find which package provides a file. dnf clean all — clean cache. On Debian/Ubuntu: apt search, apt install, apt remove, apt update, apt upgrade.

question: What are the essential rpm commands?
answer: rpm -ivh <pkg.rpm> — install with verbose and hash progress. rpm -Uvh <pkg.rpm> — upgrade. rpm -e <pkg> — erase/remove. rpm -qa — query all installed packages. rpm -qi <pkg> — query info. rpm -ql <pkg> — list files in package. rpm -qf <file> — find which package owns a file. rpm -V <pkg> — verify package integrity.

topic: Linux Bible Ch11: Linux File Permissions
question: What are Linux file permissions and how do they work?
answer: Three permission sets: USER (owner), GROUP, OTHERS. Permissions: r (read=4), w (write=2), x (execute=1). chmod 755 file sets rwxr-xr-x. chown user:group file changes owner/group. Special permissions: SUID (4, runs as owner), SGID (2, runs as group), Sticky Bit (1, only owner can delete in shared dir). Examples: chmod u+s file (SUID), chmod g+s dir (SGID), chmod +t dir (sticky bit).

question: What are ACLs and how do you manage them?
answer: ACLs (Access Control Lists) provide fine-grained permissions beyond standard ugo/rwx. setfacl -m u:username:rwx file — set user ACL. setfacl -m g:groupname:rx file — set group ACL. setfacl -x u:username file — remove user ACL. getfacl file — view ACLs. setfacl -m d:u:username:rwx dir — set default ACL for new files in directory. Requires acl package and filesystem mounted with acl option.

topic: Linux Bible Ch13: SSH Key Authentication
question: How do you set up SSH key-based authentication?
answer: 1. Generate key pair: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'comment' (or -t rsa -b 4096). 2. Copy public key to server: ssh-copy-id user@host. 3. (Manual) Add public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on server. 4. Set permissions: chmod 700 ~/.ssh, chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. 5. For extra security, disable password auth in /etc/ssh/sshd_config: PasswordAuthentication no. 6. Restart sshd: sudo systemctl restart sshd.

topic: Linux Bible Ch13: scp and rsync
question: What are the differences between scp and rsync?
answer: SCP (Secure Copy): cp over SSH. Syntax: scp file user@host:/path/. Simple, always copies entire file. RSYNC: more powerful, only transfers differences (delta algorithm). Syntax: rsync -avz file user@host:/path/. Options: -a (archive, preserve permissions), -v (verbose), -z (compress), --delete (remove files not at source), --progress (show progress). rsync can also sync local directories and works over SSH by default.

question: How is rsyslog configured on Linux?
answer: Configuration file: /etc/rsyslog.conf or /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf. Format: facility.priority action. Facilities: auth, authpriv, cron, daemon, kern, local0-7, mail, syslog, user. Priorities: debug, info, notice, warning, err, crit, alert, emerg. Examples: *.info;mail.none;authpriv.none /var/log/messages, authpriv.* /var/log/secure, mail.* /var/log/maillog. To set up a loghost: module(load='imtcp'), input(type='imtcp' port='514'), then use @hostname in client config.

question: What are the most important ip command uses?
answer: ip addr show — show all IP addresses. ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0 — add IP. ip addr del 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0 — remove IP. ip link show — show interfaces. ip link set eth0 up/down — enable/disable. ip route show — routing table. ip route add default via 192.168.1.1 — add default route. ip route add 10.0.0.0/8 via 192.168.1.1 — add specific route. ip neigh show — ARP/ND cache. The ip command replaces ifconfig, route, and arp.

question: What are the essential nmcli commands?
answer: nmcli dev status — show device status. nmcli con show — show connections. nmcli con show 'name' — show connection details. nmcli con add con-name 'eth0' ifname eth0 type ethernet — add connection. nmcli con mod 'eth0' ipv4.method manual ipv4.addr 192.168.1.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 — configure static IP. nmcli con mod 'eth0' ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8 — set DNS. nmcli con up 'eth0' — activate. nmcli con down 'eth0' — deactivate. nmcli radio wifi on/off — control Wi-Fi.

topic: Linux Bible Ch14: Network Config Files
question: What are the key Linux network configuration files?
answer: /etc/hosts — static hostname-IP mappings (used before DNS). /etc/resolv.conf — DNS resolver config (nameserver, search, domain). /etc/nsswitch.conf — name service switch (order of resolution: files dns means check hosts file first, then DNS). /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ — legacy location for interface configs (RHEL ≤8). NetworkManager stores connections in /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/.

question: How does /etc/hosts interact with DNS resolution?
answer: The /etc/nsswitch.conf file controls the order: 'hosts: files dns' means check /etc/hosts first, then query DNS. /etc/hosts format: IP_address hostname [aliases]. Example: 127.0.0.1 localhost localhost.localdomain. /etc/resolv.conf format: nameserver 8.8.8.8, search example.com (domain suffix for unqualified names). /etc/hosts was the original name resolution method before DNS.

question: What is systemd and what are its key components?
answer: systemd is the init system and service manager used by most modern Linux distributions. PID 1. Key features: parallel service startup, dependency-based service control, socket/timer activation, logging (journald). Unit types: .service (daemons), .socket (network sockets), .target (groups of units, like runlevels), .timer (scheduled tasks), .mount (filesystems), .path (file monitoring). Target examples: multi-user.target (CLI), graphical.target (with GUI), reboot.target, poweroff.target.

question: What are the essential systemctl commands?
answer: systemctl start <service> — start service. systemctl stop <service> — stop. systemctl restart <service> — restart. systemctl reload <service> — reload config. systemctl status <service> — show status. systemctl enable <service> — enable at boot. systemctl disable <service> — disable at boot. systemctl is-enabled <service> — check. systemctl list-units — list active units. systemctl list-unit-files — list all unit files and their enable state. systemctl daemon-reload — reload systemd config after adding units.

question: What are the key journalctl commands for log viewing?
answer: journalctl — view all logs. journalctl -u <service> — logs for specific service. journalctl -f — follow new logs (like tail -f). journalctl --since '1 hour ago' — time filter. journalctl --until '2025-01-01' — until time. journalctl -p err — filter by priority (emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug). journalctl -k — kernel messages. journalctl --list-boots — list boots. journalctl -b -1 — previous boot logs. journalctl -x — add explanation. journalctl -o verbose — detailed output.

topic: Linux Bible Ch17: Apache Config Directives
question: What are the key Apache HTTPD configuration directives?
answer: ServerRoot /etc/httpd — base directory. Listen 80 — port to listen on. DocumentRoot /var/www/html — web root directory. DirectoryIndex index.html — default page. <Directory /var/www/html> — directory-level config (Options, AllowOverride, Require). ErrorLog /var/log/httpd/error_log — error log. CustomLog /var/log/httpd/access_log combined — access log. ServerName www.example.com:80 — server name. Include conf.modules.d/*.conf — include other config files.

question: How do you configure SSL/TLS for Apache?
answer: 1. Install mod_ssl: dnf install mod_ssl. 2. Config file: /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf. 3. Generate self-signed cert: openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout /etc/pki/tls/private/localhost.key -out /etc/pki/tls/certs/localhost.crt -days 365 -nodes. 4. For production: generate CSR and get CA-signed cert. Key directives: SSLCertificateFile, SSLCertificateKeyFile, SSLCACertificateFile. 5. Firewall: firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent.

topic: Linux Bible Ch21: Network Troubleshooting Steps
question: What are the systematic steps for troubleshooting outgoing connections?
answer: 1. VIEW NETWORK INTERFACES: ip addr show, ip link show — verify interface is up and has IP. 2. CHECK PHYSICAL CONNECTION: ethtool eth0 (link detected), check cable/switch LED. 3. CHECK ROUTES: ip route show — verify default gateway exists. 4. CHECK HOSTNAME RESOLUTION: getent hosts <hostname>, host <name>, nslookup <name> — verify DNS resolves. 5. PING GATEWAY: ping -c 4 <gateway> — verify local connectivity. 6. TRACEROUTE: traceroute <remote> — identify where path fails. 7. CHECK FIREWALL: firewall-cmd --list-all, iptables -L -n — verify traffic not blocked.

topic: Linux Bible Ch21: Troubleshooting Incoming Connections
question: What are the systematic steps for troubleshooting incoming connections?
answer: 1. CHECK CLIENT CAN REACH SERVER: ping server_IP from client. 2. CHECK SERVICE LISTENING: ss -tulpn | grep <port> — verify service is running and listening. 3. CHECK LOCAL FIREWALL: firewall-cmd --list-all (check services/ports open). 4. CHECK SELINUX: getenforce, ausearch -m avc -ts recent — check if SELinux is blocking. 5. CHECK SERVICE ACCESS: curl http://localhost:<port> from server, then from client. 6. CHECK LOGS: journalctl -u <service>, /var/log/<service>/access_log, /var/log/messages.

question: What are the three SELinux modes and how do you manage them?
answer: 1. ENFORCING: SELinux enforces policy — access denied unless explicitly allowed. Default on RHEL/Fedora. 2. PERMISSIVE: SELinux logs violations but does not block. Use for troubleshooting. 3. DISABLED: SELinux completely off. NOT recommended — labels may not persist on reboot. Commands: getenforce — show current mode. setenforce 0 — set permissive (immediate, not persistent). setenforce 1 — set enforcing. Edit /etc/selinux/config to change permanently: SELINUX=enforcing|permissive|disabled.

question: What are SELinux security contexts and how do you manage them?
answer: Security context format: user:role:type:level (e.g., unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0). The TYPE is most important — it determines which processes can access which files. Commands: ls -Z — view file contexts. ps -Z — view process contexts. chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /var/www/html/file — change context. restorecon -v /var/www/html/file — restore default context. semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/web(/.*)?' — set default context for path. semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 — allow service on non-standard port.

question: What are SELinux booleans and how do you manage them?
answer: Booleans are on/off switches that allow specific SELinux policy changes without reloading policy. Common ones: httpd_enable_homedirs (allow Apache access to home dirs), ftpd_anon_write (allow anonymous FTP), samba_export_all_rw (Samba full access). Commands: getsebool -a — list all booleans. getsebool <name> — check specific. setsebool <name> on — enable (immediate). setsebool -P <name> on — enable persistent (survives reboot). semanage boolean -l — list with descriptions.

question: What is firewalld and how does it differ from iptables?
answer: firewalld is the dynamic firewall manager on RHEL/Fedora. It uses zones to organize rules (public, internal, trusted, dmz, block, drop). Key differences from iptables: dynamic (rules apply immediately without restart), zone-based (easier management), services instead of raw ports, runtime vs permanent configuration. firewalld uses nftables as its backend (RHEL 9+). Commands: systemctl status firewalld, firewall-cmd --state, firewall-cmd --list-all.

question: What are the essential firewall-cmd commands?
answer: firewall-cmd --get-default-zone — show default zone. firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=public — change default zone. firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http — allow HTTP (runtime). firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent — permanent. firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-port=8080/tcp — allow port. firewall-cmd --zone=public --remove-service=http — remove. firewall-cmd --list-all-zones — list all zones. firewall-cmd --reload — reload permanent config. firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent — save runtime to permanent. firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-source=192.168.1.0/24 — allow subnet.

question: What are the essential ufw commands on Ubuntu/Debian?
answer: ufw enable — enable firewall. ufw disable — disable. ufw status verbose — show status and rules. ufw default deny incoming — default policy. ufw default allow outgoing — default outgoing. ufw allow http — allow service by name (from /etc/services). ufw allow 80/tcp — allow port. ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 22 — allow SSH from subnet. ufw deny 23/tcp — deny port. ufw delete allow http — remove rule. ufw reload — reload. ufw logging on — enable logging.

question: What is nftables and how is it different from iptables?
answer: nftables is the successor to iptables, providing a unified framework for packet filtering, NAT, and packet mangling. Single nft command replaces iptables, ip6tables, arptables, ebtables. Uses a simpler syntax with address families (ip, ip6, inet, arp, bridge). Key advantage: performance (single pass through ruleset), atomic rule replacement, better error reporting. Example: nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept. RHEL 9+ and Fedora use nftables as the default backend for firewalld.

topic: Linux Bible Ch27: Podman vs Docker
question: What is Podman and how does it compare to Docker?
answer: Podman is a daemonless container engine for Linux. Key differences from Docker: no daemon (runs as rootless by default), Docker-compatible CLI, supports pods (like Kubernetes), built into RHEL/Fedora. Commands: podman pull <image>, podman run -it <image> /bin/bash, podman ps (running containers), podman ps -a (all), podman images (list images), podman exec -it <container> /bin/bash (shell into running container), podman stop <container>, podman rm <container>, podman rmi <image>.

question: How do you build a container image?
answer: Create a Dockerfile (also used by Podman) with instructions: FROM <base-image> (e.g., fedora:latest), RUN <command> (e.g., dnf install -y httpd), COPY <src> <dest>, EXPOSE <port>, CMD or ENTRYPOINT (startup command). Build: podman build -t myimage . (note the dot for current directory). Run: podman run -d -p 8080:80 myimage. Multi-stage builds allow smaller final images.

question: Compare systemd and SysVinit initialization systems.
correct_answer: systemd: Modern init system (PID 1) used by most distributions. Parallel service startup (faster boot). Dependency-based (unit files declare dependencies). Socket/timer activation (start services on demand). Uses systemctl command. Logs managed by journald (binary, structured). Units: .service, .socket, .target, .timer. SysVinit: Legacy init system from UNIX System V. Sequential startup (slower). Runlevel-based (0-6). Uses service and chkconfig commands. Logs to text files via syslog. Init scripts are shell scripts in /etc/init.d/. Simpler but less flexible. Most distributions have migrated from SysVinit to systemd.
distractors: SysVinit is faster than systemd because it is simpler
systemd and SysVinit are completely incompatible
SysVinit uses the same unit file format as systemd
explanation: systemd has become the standard (RHEL 7+, Fedora, Ubuntu 15+, Debian 8+). SysVinit backward compatibility is maintained through wrapper scripts.

topic: firewalld vs UFW vs iptables vs nftables
question: Compare Linux firewall management tools: firewalld, UFW, iptables, and nftables.
correct_answer: iptables: Legacy command-line firewall utility, uses rulesets with tables (filter, nat, mangle). Complex syntax, linear processing. Being replaced by nftables. nftables: Modern replacement for iptables. Single command for IPv4/IPv6/ARP. Simpler syntax, atomic rule replacement, better performance. Default backend on RHEL 9+. firewalld: Dynamic firewall manager (RHEL/Fedora). Zone-based (public, internal, dmz, trusted). Services and ports instead of raw rules. Runtime + permanent config. Backend: nftables (RHEL 9+) or iptables (older). CLI: firewall-cmd. UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall): Simplified firewall for Ubuntu/Debian. Wrapper around iptables/nftables. Easy syntax: ufw allow 80/tcp. Best for desktops/simple servers.
distractors: UFW and firewalld can be used interchangeably on any Linux distribution
iptables and nftables have the exact same syntax
firewalld directly configures kernel firewall rules without any backend
explanation: Choose based on distribution: firewalld for RHEL/Fedora, UFW for Ubuntu/Debian. nftables is the future; iptables is deprecated.

topic: SELinux Modes: Enforcing vs Permissive vs Disabled
question: Compare the three SELinux operational modes.
correct_answer: ENFORCING: SELinux policy is actively enforced. Access is denied unless explicitly allowed by policy. The default and recommended mode on RHEL/Fedora. Security contexts are properly labeled. Best for production. PERMISSIVE: SELinux policy is NOT enforced — access is allowed. But violations are logged to the audit log (/var/log/audit/audit.log). Used for troubleshooting policy violations. Use 'setenforce 0' to enter this mode temporarily. DISABLED: SELinux is completely turned off. No policy loaded, no logging. NOT recommended — when re-enabled, file system relabeling is required because security contexts may be incorrect. Changing from disabled to enforcing requires a reboot and full relabel.
distractors: Permissive mode is safe for production because it still blocks some violations
Disabling SELinux improves security because it reduces complexity
SELinux enforcing mode is the same as having no security restrictions
explanation: For troubleshooting: switch to permissive, check audit log, fix the issue, switch back to enforcing. Never leave a system in permissive or disabled.

question: Compare SCP, rsync, and SFTP for file transfer.
correct_answer: SCP (Secure Copy): Simplest — scp file user@host:/path/. Always copies ALL data (no delta). Good for one-off transfers. Single file or recursive directory (-r). SSH-based. RSYNC: Most powerful — rsync -avz file user@host:/path/. Delta algorithm (only transfers differences). Bandwidth efficient for repeated transfers/syncs. Features: compression (-z), preserve permissions (-a), delete extras (--delete), progress (--progress), exclude patterns (--exclude). SSH-based by default, also works with rsync daemon (port 873). SFTP: Interactive — sftp user@host. Like FTP over SSH. Supports: ls, cd, get, put, mkdir, rm. Good for interactive browsing. Also: scp -o sftp for SFTP-only server.
distractors: SCP is more efficient than rsync for repeated transfers
SFTP is faster than rsync for large transfers
rsync cannot transfer files over SSH
explanation: For backups/syncs: rsync. For one-off downloads: scp. For interactive browsing: sftp. All use SSH for encryption.

prompt: Arrange the steps to set up SSH key-based authentication in the correct order.
correct_sequence: Generate key pair on client: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'comment'
Copy public key to server: ssh-copy-id user@server (or manually add to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys)
Set correct permissions on server: chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
Test key-based login: ssh user@server (should log in without password prompt)
(Optional) Disable password authentication on server: edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config, set PasswordAuthentication no
(Optional) Restart SSH service: sudo systemctl restart sshd
explanation: Key permissions are critical — if ~/.ssh or authorized_keys have wrong permissions, SSH will fall back to password auth or refuse connection.

prompt: Arrange the steps for troubleshooting an outgoing network connection in the correct order.
correct_sequence: Check network interface status: ip addr show, ip link show (is interface up?)
Check physical connectivity: ethtool eth0 (link detected?), cable/switch LEDs
Check routing table: ip route show (does default gateway exist?)
Check DNS resolution: getent hosts <hostname>, host <name> (does name resolve?)
Ping default gateway: ping -c 4 <gateway> (can you reach local network?)
Ping remote host by IP: ping -c 4 8.8.8.8 (can you reach Internet?)
Ping remote host by name: ping -c 4 google.com (does DNS work end-to-end?)
Traceroute to identify where failure occurs: traceroute google.com
explanation: Follow the OSI model bottom-up: physical → link → network → transport. Each step isolates the problem to a specific layer.

question: A Linux service fails to start. What steps do you take to diagnose the issue?
correct_answer: 1. Check service status: systemctl status <service> (shows exit code, recent logs). 2. View full logs: journalctl -u <service> -n 50 --no-pager (last 50 lines). 3. Check config syntax: for Apache (httpd -t), for SSH (sshd -t), for Nginx (nginx -t). 4. Check for missing dependencies: ldd $(which <binary>) for missing libraries. 5. Check SELinux: getenforce, then ausearch -m avc -ts recent for denials. 6. Check ports: ss -tulpn | grep <port> (is something else using the port?). 7. Check filesystem: ls -la /var/lib/<service> (permissions, missing directories). 8. Run manually: sudo -u <user> /usr/sbin/<binary> to see actual error output.
explanation: Always check journalctl first — it captures the most useful diagnostic information. SELinux denials are a very common cause of mysterious failures.

question: Apache is running and listening on port 80, but external clients cannot connect. What could be blocking access?
correct_answer: Three common causes: 1. FIREWALL blocking incoming port: check firewall-cmd --list-all (RHEL/Fedora) or ufw status (Ubuntu). Add rule: firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent or ufw allow 80/tcp. 2. SELINUX blocking: check 'getenforce' (if Enforcing, check 'ausearch -m avc -ts recent' for denials). Common fix: setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on or restorecon -v /var/www/html. 3. Apache LISTENING on wrong interface: check 'ss -tulpn | grep 80' — if listening on 127.0.0.1:80 instead of 0.0.0.0:80, change Listen directive in /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf. Also check: cloud firewall (AWS security group, Azure NSG), router port forwarding.
explanation: Check local first (curl http://localhost), then local network (curl http://server-ip from another host), then external. This isolates the layer.

question: A Linux server can ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot resolve hostnames. What is the issue and how do you fix it?
correct_answer: DNS resolution is failing. Steps: 1. Check /etc/resolv.conf — does it contain valid nameserver entries? 'nameserver 8.8.8.8' or 'nameserver 1.1.1.1'. 2. Check /etc/nsswitch.conf — 'hosts: files dns' ensures DNS is consulted after /etc/hosts. 3. Test with dig: 'dig google.com' or 'host google.com'. 4. Test with nslookup: 'nslookup google.com'. 5. Check if DNS server is reachable: 'ping -c 2 8.8.8.8' (DNS server IP). 6. Check if NetworkManager overwrote resolv.conf: check if /etc/resolv.conf is a symlink to /run/NetworkManager/resolv.conf. 7. Common fixes: restart NetworkManager ('systemctl restart NetworkManager'), check DHCP provides correct DNS, manually set DNS in /etc/resolv.conf or via nmcli: 'nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8'.
explanation: If /etc/resolv.conf is managed by NetworkManager, manual edits will be overwritten. Use nmcli or the network config file instead.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch1
question: What is the Linux kernel and what are its main functions?
answer: The kernel is the core component of an OS that manages the computer's hardware. Main functions: (1) allocating memory for programs, (2) allocating CPU time (process scheduling), (3) controlling access to hard disks and other storage, (4) enabling programs to use the network. The kernel is loaded at boot time and remains in memory, handling requests from user applications via system calls.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch1
question: What are the three main components that make up an operating system?
answer: 1. KERNEL: manages hardware resources (CPU, memory, disk, network). 2. UTILITIES: system programs that perform specific tasks (file managers, text editors, configuration tools). Many come from the GNU project. 3. APPLICATIONS: user-facing programs (web browsers, office suites, games). Linux is technically just the kernel; a complete OS includes all three layers combined into a distribution.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch1
question: Compare command-line interface (CLI) and graphical user interface (GUI).
answer: CLI: text-based, user types commands, more efficient for automation/scripting, uses fewer resources, essential for remote administration (SSH). GUI: visual with windows/icons/menus, more intuitive for beginners, uses more resources, limited automation. Linux supports both — servers often run CLI-only; desktops use GUI with terminal access.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch1
question: What are the three main distribution families and their package systems?
answer: 1. DEBIAN family: Debian, Ubuntu, Mint, Kali. Uses DEB packages (.deb) and apt/dpkg tools. 2. RED HAT family: RHEL, Fedora, CentOS. Uses RPM packages (.rpm) and dnf/yum/rpm tools. 3. SUSE family: openSUSE, SLES. Uses RPM packages with zypper tool. All distributions share the same Linux kernel but differ in package management, default software, and release cycles.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch1
question: What are the three cloud computing service models?
answer: 1. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): vendor provides virtual servers, storage, networking. Customer manages OS and applications. Example: AWS EC2. 2. PaaS (Platform as a Service): vendor provides OS + infrastructure. Customer deploys applications only. Example: Google App Engine. 3. SaaS (Software as a Service): vendor provides fully functional application. Customer just uses it. Example: Gmail, Office 365.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch2
question: What are the four essential freedoms defined by the Free Software Foundation?
answer: Freedom 0: run the program for any purpose. Freedom 1: study and modify the source code. Freedom 2: redistribute copies. Freedom 3: distribute modified versions. These define 'free software' — free as in speech, not as in beer. Software that grants these freedoms is called 'free software' or 'copyleft' software.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch2
question: What are the key principles of the Open Source Initiative (OSI)?
answer: The OSI defines 10 criteria for open source certification: (1) free redistribution, (2) source code must be included, (3) derived works allowed, (4) source code integrity respected, (5) no discrimination against persons/groups, (6) no discrimination against fields of endeavor, (7) license applies automatically, (8) not product-specific, (9) no restrictions on other software, (10) technology-neutral.

topic: LPI Ch2: GPL v2 vs v3
source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch2
question: What are the differences between GPLv2 (1991) and GPLv3 (2007)?
answer: GPLv2: the original copyleft license, requires source code distribution with binaries. GPLv3: updated for modern software issues — adds anti-tivoization clause (cannot restrict hardware from running modified versions), better patent protection (explicit patent grant), compatibility with other licenses (Apache 2.0), and digital restrictions management (DRM) restrictions.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch2
question: What are permissive open source licenses versus copyleft?
answer: Permissive licenses (BSD, MIT, Apache 2.0): allow users to copy, modify, and distribute the software WITHOUT requiring source code distribution of modifications. Can be incorporated into proprietary software. Copyleft licenses (GPL): require that modified versions also be distributed under the same license — source code must remain open. Apache 2.0 includes an explicit patent grant not found in BSD/MIT.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch3
question: What type of kernel does Linux use and what does that mean?
answer: Linux uses a monolithic kernel design. All OS services (process management, memory management, file systems, device drivers) run in kernel space as a single large process. This differs from microkernel designs where services run in user space. Advantages: performance (no message passing overhead). Disadvantage: a bug in any driver can crash the entire system.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch3
question: What is preemptive multitasking and how does Linux implement it?
answer: Preemptive multitasking: the kernel controls CPU time allocation — it can preempt (interrupt) a running process and give CPU time to another process. Each process gets a time slice (quantum). This differs from cooperative multitasking where processes voluntarily yield the CPU. Linux's scheduler (CFS — Completely Fair Scheduler) ensures all processes get fair CPU access.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch4
question: What are the major Linux desktop environments?
answer: GNOME: default on Fedora/RHEL/Ubuntu, modern and streamlined. KDE Plasma: customizable, traditional desktop feel, default on openSUSE. Xfce: lightweight, good for older hardware. LXDE/LXQt: very lightweight, for low-resource systems. MATE: GNOME 2 fork, traditional look. Cinnamon: default on Linux Mint, traditional with modern features. Each provides a window manager, panels, file manager, and settings tools.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch4
question: What are the common network server protocols and their port numbers?
answer: FTP (20-21): file transfer. SSH (22): encrypted remote login. Telnet (23): unencrypted remote access. SMTP (25): email sending. DNS (53): name resolution. HTTP (80): web traffic. POP3 (110): email retrieval. IMAP (143): email with server-side storage. HTTPS (443): encrypted web traffic. SMB/CIFS (137-139, 445): Windows file/print sharing. NFS (2049): Linux file sharing.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch4
question: What is the difference between compiled and interpreted programming languages?
answer: Compiled languages (C, C++, Go): source code is compiled into machine code before execution. Faster execution, more complex development. Interpreted languages (Python, Perl, Bash): source code is executed by an interpreter at runtime. Slower execution, easier development and debugging. Some languages (Java, C#) use a hybrid approach — compiled to bytecode, then interpreted by a virtual machine.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch5
question: What are the nine manual page sections in Linux?
answer: Section 1: User commands (runnable by any user). Section 2: System calls (kernel interfaces). Section 3: Library functions (C library). Section 4: Device files (/dev). Section 5: File formats (/etc/passwd, /etc/fstab). Section 6: Games. Section 7: Miscellaneous (conventions, standards). Section 8: System administration commands (root-only). Section 9: Kernel routines. man 5 passwd opens section 5; man passwd opens lowest-numbered match.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch5
question: What is the difference between apropos and whatis?
answer: whatis: searches for EXACT keyword match in man page NAME sections. Returns one-line summary. Example: whatis passwd. apropos: searches for KEYWORD in man page NAME sections using substring match. Returns all matching man pages. Example: apropos passwd. Both use the man page database (mandb). apropos is equivalent to 'man -k'.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch5
question: What sections does a typical man page contain?
answer: NAME: command name and one-line description. SYNOPSIS: command syntax with options ([] for optional, <> for required). DESCRIPTION: detailed explanation. OPTIONS: list of command options. FILES: related configuration files. EXAMPLES: usage examples. SEE ALSO: related commands and documentation. AUTHOR: who wrote it. BUGS: known issues.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch5
question: What are the key bash shell productivity features?
answer: 1. COMMAND COMPLETION (Tab key): completes commands, files, directories, variables. Double Tab shows all matches. 2. COMMAND HISTORY (up/down arrows): scroll through previous commands. history command shows list. !! repeats last command. !n repeats command #n. 3. ALIASES: create shortcuts (alias ll='ls -l'). 4. WILDCARDS: * (any chars), ? (single char), [abc] (character class). 5. VARIABLES: $PATH determines where shell looks for executables.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch5
question: How do you navigate info pages?
answer: Info pages are hypertext documentation maintained by the GNU project. Navigation: arrow keys to move between lines, Enter to follow a link, N/P to go to next/previous page, U to go up one level, Q to quit, Tab to jump between links. Info is often more detailed than man pages. Run 'info <command>' to view. Some commands only have info documentation.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch6
question: What are the common CPU architectures supported by Linux?
answer: x86 (32-bit): Intel/AMD CPUs from the 80386 onward. AMD64/EM64T (64-bit): current standard for desktop/server, also called x86-64. ARM: used in smartphones, Raspberry Pi, embedded devices. MIPS: used in embedded systems/routers. PowerPC: used in older Macs, some servers. Linux supports more architectures than any other OS. Use 'lscpu' or 'uname -m' to identify your CPU architecture.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch6
question: How does Linux organize data on disks?
answer: Disks are divided into partitions (MBR: 4 primary or 3 primary + extended, GPT: up to 128). Tools: fdisk (MBR), gdisk (GPT), parted. Each partition is formatted with a filesystem. Common Linux filesystems: ext4 (default for most), XFS (scalable, RHEL default), btrfs (advanced features like snapshots), swap (virtual memory). Mount points attach filesystems to the directory tree: 'mount /dev/sda1 /mnt', /etc/fstab defines permanent mounts.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch6
question: How does Linux manage hardware drivers?
answer: Linux includes most drivers directly in the kernel. Additional drivers can be loaded as kernel modules. Key commands: lsmod (list loaded modules), modprobe (load/remove modules), modinfo (module details). Modules are stored in /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/. The kernel detects hardware at boot and loads appropriate drivers automatically (udev for hotplug devices). For proprietary drivers, use DKMS to rebuild across kernel updates.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch7
question: What are the key directories in the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)?
answer: /bin — essential user binaries (ls, cp, mv). /sbin — essential system binaries (fdisk, mkfs). /usr — non-essential programs and data (largest directory). /etc — configuration files. /var — variable data (logs, mail, databases). /tmp — temporary files (may be cleared on reboot). /home — user home directories. /root — root user's home. /dev — device files. /proc — running process information (virtual filesystem). /boot — boot loader files (kernel, initramfs).

topic: LPI Ch7: Hard vs Symbolic Links
source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch7
question: What is the difference between hard links and symbolic (soft) links?
answer: HARD LINK (ln target linkname): shares the same inode as the target. Both filenames point to identical data. Cannot cross filesystems. Cannot link directories. Deleting original doesn't affect link (data remains if at least one link exists). SYMBOLIC LINK (ln -s target linkname): special file that points to target by name (path). Can cross filesystems. Can link directories. If target is deleted, link becomes broken (dangling). Use 'ls -i' to see inode numbers.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch7
question: What wildcards does the bash shell support for filename matching?
answer: *(asterisk): matches zero or more characters. Example: 'ls *.txt' finds all .txt files. ? (question mark): matches exactly one character. Example: 'ls file?' matches file1, fileA but not file10. [] (brackets): matches one character from a set or range. Example: 'ls file[0-9]' matches file0-file9. [!] or [^]: matches characters NOT in the set. Example: 'ls file[!a-z]' matches file1, fileA but not filea.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch8
question: What are the most useful grep options?
answer: grep searches for patterns in files. Key options: -i (case-insensitive), -v (invert match), -r (recursive through directories), -n (show line numbers), -l (list filenames only), -c (count matches), -E (extended regex — allows |, +, ?, {}), -o (show only matched text). Examples: grep -r 'ERROR' /var/log/, grep -E '(error|warning)' file.log, grep -v '^#' /etc/ssh/sshd_config.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch8
question: How do I/O redirection operators work in bash?
answer: > file — redirect stdout to file (overwrite). >> file — redirect stdout to file (append). 2> file — redirect stderr to file. 2>> file — redirect stderr (append). &> file — redirect both stdout and stderr. 2>&1 — redirect stderr to stdout. < file — use file as stdin. << delimiter — heredoc (inline input). Example: 'grep -r 'error' /var/log/ > errors.txt 2> /dev/null'.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch8
question: How do pipes work in Linux?
answer: The pipe operator (|) connects stdout of one command to stdin of another. Example: 'ls -l | grep '^d' | wc -l' counts directories. Pipes enable the UNIX philosophy of combining small, focused tools. Common pipeline: 'ps aux | grep firefox | grep -v grep | awk '{print $2}''. The tee command (tee file) copies pipe output to a file while also passing it through: 'command | tee log.txt | nextcommand'.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch8
question: What are the essential tar command options?
answer: tar (tape archive) bundles files into a single archive. Common operations: -c (create archive), -x (extract), -t (list contents). Key options: -f (specify archive filename), -v (verbose), -z (gzip compression, .tar.gz), -j (bzip2, .tar.bz2), -J (xz, .tar.xz). Examples: 'tar -czf archive.tar.gz /path/to/files' (create), 'tar -xzf archive.tar.gz' (extract), 'tar -tf archive.tar.gz' (list). Always use -f last as it takes an argument.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch8
question: What are the common Linux compression tools?
answer: gzip (.gz): most common, moderate compression, fast. bzip2 (.bz2): better compression than gzip, slower. xz (.xz): best compression ratio, slowest. zip (.zip): cross-platform, archives+compresses in one step. All compress individual files only (use tar to bundle first, then compress). Use zcat/zless to view compressed files. Examples: 'gzip file', 'bzip2 -k file' (keep original), 'xz -9 file' (maximum compression).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch9
question: Compare RPM and DEB package management systems.
answer: RPM (.rpm): used by Red Hat, Fedora, CentOS, SUSE. Low-level tool: rpm (install, query, verify). High-level tools: dnf (modern, RHEL 8+), yum (legacy, RHEL 7). DEB (.deb): used by Debian, Ubuntu, Mint. Low-level tool: dpkg. High-level tool: apt (or apt-get). Both systems handle dependencies, track installed files, verify package integrity. Commands are similar: dnf install = apt install, dnf remove = apt remove, dnf update = apt upgrade.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch9
question: What are the key ps command options for viewing processes?
answer: ps -ef: full listing showing UID, PID, PPID, C, STIME, TTY, TIME, CMD. ps aux: similar output (BSD-style). ps -u username: show processes for specific user. ps --forest: show process tree (parent-child relationships). ps ax | grep pattern: find specific process. ps -o pid,ppid,cmd: custom output format. Without options, ps shows only processes attached to the current terminal. The PPID (parent PID) column helps identify process relationships.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch9
question: What are the interactive commands within top?
answer: top shows real-time process information. Interactive keys: h (help), k (kill a process by PID), q (quit), M (sort by memory usage), P (sort by CPU usage), N (sort by PID), r (renice a process), u (filter by user), 1 (toggle per-CPU stats). Fields: PID, USER, PR (priority), NI (nice value), VIRT (virtual memory), RES (physical memory), SHR (shared memory), S (status: R=running, S=sleeping, Z=zombie), %CPU, %MEM, TIME+, COMMAND.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch9
question: What does the free command show and how to interpret its output?
answer: free shows memory usage. Columns: total, used, free, shared, buff/cache, available. The 'available' column is the most useful — it estimates how much memory is available for new processes (includes reclaimable cache). Buff/cache is memory used by kernel for file caching (can be freed when needed). Use 'free -h' for human-readable output. Also check /proc/meminfo for detailed memory information.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch9
question: What is the kernel ring buffer and how do you view it?
answer: The kernel ring buffer stores kernel-generated messages (hardware detection, driver messages, errors). It's a circular buffer in memory — old messages are overwritten. View with 'dmesg' command. Use 'dmesg | less' to page through, 'dmesg | grep sda' to find disk-related messages. Log files in /var/log/ also capture these messages. The ring buffer is especially useful for diagnosing hardware issues that occur during boot.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch9
question: Where does Linux store system log files?
answer: Main log directory: /var/log/. Common files: /var/log/messages (general system messages, default on some distros), /var/log/syslog (Debian/Ubuntu general log), /var/log/secure (authentication/security messages), /var/log/maillog or /var/log/mail.log (email server logs), /var/log/httpd/ (Apache access/error logs), /var/log/dmesg (kernel ring buffer at boot), /var/log/boot.log (boot messages). journalctl views the systemd journal (binary log format).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch10
question: What are the essential nano keyboard shortcuts?
answer: nano is a simple text-mode editor. Ctrl+O (WriteOut): save file. Ctrl+X (Exit): exit (prompts to save if modified). Ctrl+K (Cut Text): cut entire line. Ctrl+U (Uncut Text): paste. Ctrl+W (Where Is): search. Ctrl+Backslash (Replace): search and replace. Ctrl+G (Get Help): show help. Ctrl+C (Cursor Position): show cursor position. Ctrl+V (Next Page): page down. Ctrl+Y (Previous Page): page up. Commands shown at bottom of screen (^ = Ctrl, M- = Alt).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch10
question: What are the three modes of the vi editor?
answer: 1. COMMAND MODE (default on open): keyboard keys execute commands — h/j/k/l (move), x (delete char), dd (delete line), yy (copy line), p (paste), / (search). Press Esc from any mode to return here. 2. INSERT MODE: type text. Enter with i (insert before cursor), a (append after), o (open new line below), O (open above), I (insert at line start), A (append at line end). 3. EX/LINE MODE: enter commands with : (colon) — :w (save), :q (quit), :wq (save+quit), :q! (force quit), :set number (show line numbers)

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch11
question: What is the basic structure of a bash shell script?
answer: 1. SHEBANG: first line is '#!/bin/sh' or '#!/bin/bash' — tells system which interpreter to use. 2. COMMANDS: list of commands in execution order. 3. VARIABLES: name=value, referenced with $name. 4. ARGUMENTS: $1, $2, ..., $@ (all args), $# (count), $0 (script name). 5. CONDITIONALS: if/then/elif/else/fi, test with [] or [[]]. 6. LOOPS: for/while/until. 7. EXIT STATUS: 'exit 0' for success, non-zero for error. 8. Make executable: chmod +x script.sh. Run with ./script.sh.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch11
question: What are the common test operators in shell scripts?
answer: File tests: -f file (exists and regular), -d file (directory), -e file (exists), -r file (readable), -w file (writable), -x file (executable), -s file (non-empty). String tests: -z str (empty), -n str (non-empty), str1 = str2 (equal), str1 != str2 (not equal). Numeric tests: -eq (equal), -ne (not equal), -lt (less than), -gt (greater than), -le (less/equal), -ge (greater/equal). Combine with && (AND) and || (OR).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch12
question: What are the seven fields in /etc/passwd?
answer: Format: username:password:UID:GID:comment:home_directory:shell. 1. Username: login name. 2. Password: x (password stored in /etc/shadow). 3. UID: user ID number (0=root, 1-999=system, 1000+=regular). 4. GID: primary group ID. 5. Comment/GECOS: full name, contact info. 6. Home directory: user's home (e.g., /home/username). 7. Shell: login shell (e.g., /bin/bash, /sbin/nologin for system accounts).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch12
question: What are the fields in /etc/shadow?
answer: Format: username:hashed_password:lastchange:minage:maxage:warn:inactive:expire:flag. 1. Username: matches /etc/passwd. 2. Hashed password: salted hash ($type$salt$hash). !! or * means account locked/no password. 3. Last change: days since Epoch (Jan 1, 1970) password was last changed. 4. Min age: days before password can be changed. 5. Max age: days after which password must be changed. 6. Warn: days warning before expiration. 7. Inactive: days after expiration before account is disabled. 8. Expire: account expiration date (Epoch format).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch12
question: What are the Linux UID ranges and their purposes?
answer: UID 0: root — superuser with full system access. UIDs 1-999: system accounts — used by services and daemons (sshd, apache, mysql). No login shell, no password. UIDs 1000+: regular user accounts — normal users with restricted privileges. The exact cutoff varies by distribution (some use 500 or 1000). View with 'id username'. The /etc/login.defs file defines UID_MIN and UID_MAX for new accounts.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch12
question: Compare su and sudo for acquiring root privileges.
answer: su (switch user): 'su -' switches to root (requires root password). Gives full root shell. Less secure because the root password must be shared. sudo: 'sudo command' runs a single command as root (requires user's password). Configured in /etc/sudoers (edit with visudo). More secure: granular permissions (can allow specific commands only), audit trail (logged), no need to share root password. Modern Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Fedora) disable root login and use sudo exclusively.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch13
question: What are the common useradd command options?
answer: useradd creates a new user. Key options: -c 'comment' (full name), -d /home/dir (home directory), -m (create home directory), -u UID (specific UID), -g group (primary group), -G group1,group2 (supplementary groups), -s /bin/bash (login shell), -e YYYY-MM-DD (account expiry), -f N (inactive days after password expires). The user's password must be set separately with 'passwd username'. Default values come from /etc/default/useradd and /etc/login.defs.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch13
question: How do you set password aging policies in Linux?
answer: Use the chage command: chage -l username (list aging info). chage -M 90 username (max days), -m 7 (min days), -W 14 (warning days), -I 5 (inactive days), -E YYYY-MM-DD (expire date). chage -d 0 username forces password change on next login. System-wide defaults: /etc/login.defs defines PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, PASS_WARN_AGE. Password hashes: stored in /etc/shadow (SHA-512 by default, $6$ prefix).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch13
question: What are the key group management commands?
answer: groupadd -g GID groupname (create with specific GID). groupmod -n newname oldname (rename), -g GID groupname (change GID). groupdel groupname (delete). groups username (show user's group membership). usermod -aG groupname username (add user to supplementary group). gpasswd -a username groupname (add user), -d username groupname (remove). newgrp groupname (log in with new primary group). /etc/group stores group definitions (format: groupname:password:GID:userlist).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch14
question: What do the three permission sets (owner/group/other) each allow?
answer: Each file/directory has three permission triads (rwx): OWNER (first triad): permissions for the file's owner. GROUP (second): permissions for members of the file's group. OTHER/World (third): permissions for everyone else. For files: r (read content), w (modify content), x (execute as program). For directories: r (list contents), w (create/delete files in dir), x (enter directory and access files). Execute on a directory is required to access any files within it.

topic: LPI Ch14: chmod Symbolic vs Octal
source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch14
question: What are the two ways to use chmod and examples of each?
answer: SYMBOLIC: chmod [ugoa][+-=][rwx] file. Who: u=owner, g=group, o=other, a=all. Operation: +=add, -=remove, ==set exactly. Examples: chmod a+x file (all get execute), chmod ug=rw file (owner+group get read+write), chmod o-rwx file (others get nothing). OCTAL: chmod NNN file where each digit is sum: r=4, w=2, x=1. Examples: chmod 755 (rwxr-xr-x), 700 (rwx------), 644 (rw-r--r--), 600 (rw-------).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch14
question: How does umask determine default permissions?
answer: umask subtracts permissions from the maximum default: 666 for files (no execute), 777 for directories. Common umask values: 022 (default) removes write for group+other → files 644 (rw-r--r--), dirs 755 (rwxr-xr-x). 002 removes write for other only → files 664, dirs 775 (group collaboration). 077 removes all for group+other → files 600, dirs 700 (private). View current umask with 'umask' command. Set with 'umask 027' in shell config (/etc/profile, ~/.bashrc).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch14
question: What are SUID, SGID, and Sticky Bit?
answer: SUID (Set User ID, chmod u+s, octal 4xxx): program runs with file owner's privileges. Example: /usr/bin/passwd has SUID (rwsr-xr-x) so regular users can modify /etc/shadow. SGID (Set Group ID, chmod g+s, octal 2xxx): on files — runs with group privileges; on directories — new files inherit directory's group. Sticky Bit (chmod +t, octal 1xxx): on directories — only file owners can delete their files. Example: /tmp has sticky bit (drwxrwxrwt).

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch15
question: How do you use the ip command to manage network interfaces?
answer: ip address show (or ip a): show all IP addresses. ip address add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0: assign IP. ip address del 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0: remove IP. ip link set eth0 up/down: enable/disable interface. ip route show: display routing table. ip route add default via 192.168.1.1: set default gateway. ip route add 10.0.0.0/8 via 192.168.1.1: add specific route. The ip command replaces older tools (ifconfig, route, arp) in one unified utility.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch15
question: How do you use ifconfig to configure network interfaces?
answer: ifconfig: display all active interfaces. ifconfig -a: show all (including down). ifconfig eth0 192.168.1.10 netmask 255.255.255.0: set IP and netmask. ifconfig eth0 up/down: enable/disable. ifconfig eth0: show specific interface. Note: ifconfig is deprecated in favor of the ip command. Many modern distros don't install it by default. It's still commonly used for quick checks and in scripts on older systems.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch15
question: What are the steps for basic network troubleshooting in Linux?
answer: 1. VERIFY INTERFACE: ip addr show (is interface up? has IP?). 2. CHECK LINK: ethtool eth0 (link detected?). 3. CHECK ROUTING: ip route show (default gateway exists?). 4. PING GATEWAY: ping -c 4 gateway-ip (local connectivity). 5. PING REMOTE: ping -c 4 8.8.8.8 (Internet connectivity). 6. CHECK DNS: host google.com, dig google.com, nslookup google.com (name resolution). 7. CHECK LISTENING: ss -tulpn (what's listening?). 8. CHECK LOGS: journalctl for errors.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch15
question: Compare netstat and ss commands.
answer: netstat: traditional tool for network statistics. Lists open connections, routing tables, interface statistics. Options: -t (TCP), -u (UDP), -l (listening), -n (numeric), -p (program). Deprecated on many distros. ss (socket statistics): modern replacement, faster, more detailed. Same option conventions: ss -tulpn. Shows socket-to-process mapping. Both display similar information but ss is preferred on newer systems.

source: LPI Linux Essentials Study Guide - Ch15
question: How does Linux resolve hostnames to IP addresses?
answer: Resolution order is defined in /etc/nsswitch.conf: 'hosts: files dns' means check /etc/hosts first, then DNS. /etc/hosts: static IP-to-hostname mappings (127.0.0.1 localhost). /etc/resolv.conf: DNS server configuration (nameserver 8.8.8.8, search example.com). Query tools: host (simple), dig (detailed), nslookup (interactive). DNS cache: systemd-resolved, dnsmasq, or nscd can cache DNS queries for performance.

question: Compare Linux, Windows, and macOS operating systems.
correct_answer: LINUX: Open source (GPL), free, many distributions (Fedora, Ubuntu), monolithic kernel, X11/Wayland GUI, package managers (apt, dnf), strong CLI/scripting, runs on anything (x86, ARM, mainframe), dominant on servers/cloud/supercomputers. WINDOWS: Proprietary (Microsoft), paid license, single vendor, NT kernel, Win32/Win64 GUI, .exe/.msi installers, GUI-focused with PowerShell, x86/ARM, dominant on desktops. macOS: Proprietary (Apple), hardware-bound, XNU hybrid kernel, Aqua GUI, .dmg/.pkg installers, UNIX-certified (BSD foundation), zsh shell, limited to Apple hardware, popular with developers/designers.
distractors: Linux and macOS are identical because both are based on UNIX
Windows has better security than Linux because it has more users
Linux cannot run graphical applications
explanation: Linux dominates servers (96% of top 1M servers), Android (Linux-based) dominates mobile. macOS is UNIX-certified but not open source. Windows dominates desktops.

topic: GPL vs BSD vs MIT Licenses
question: Compare GPL, BSD, and MIT open source licenses.
correct_answer: GPL (GNU General Public License): Strong copyleft — modified versions MUST also be distributed under GPL. Source code must be provided. Most restrictive of the three. Used by: Linux kernel, GNU tools, Git. BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) License: Permissive — allows use in proprietary software with minimal restrictions. Requires attribution (copyright notice). Two variants: 2-clause (no endorsement clause) and 3-clause (adds endorsement restriction). MIT License: Very permissive — allows use in proprietary software. Only requires attribution (copyright notice). Simpler and shorter than BSD. Most permissive. Used by: Node.js, React, jQuery. COMMONALITY: All three allow free use, modification, and distribution.
distractors: BSD and MIT licenses require modified source code to be published
The GPL allows proprietary software to include GPL code without restriction
All three licenses are functionally identical
explanation: Key difference: copyleft (GPL) vs permissive (BSD/MIT). GPL ensures modifications stay free. BSD/MIT allow closing the source.

question: Compare hard links and symbolic (soft) links in Linux.
correct_answer: HARD LINK (ln target link): Same inode number as target — both names point to identical data. Cannot span filesystems (must be on same partition). Cannot link directories. No size overhead (just another directory entry). If original is deleted, data remains accessible through the link. All links are equal — no 'original'. SYMBOLIC LINK (ln -s target link): Different inode — special file that stores the target's pathname. Can span filesystems. Can link directories. Small size overhead (path string). If target is deleted, link becomes 'dangling/broken'. Original and link are distinct. Use 'ls -li' to see inode numbers. Symlinks are much more common in practice.
distractors: Hard links can link to files on any filesystem
Symbolic links and hard links behave identically when the original is deleted
Deleting a hard link also deletes the original file
explanation: Hard links share the same data blocks on disk. Symlinks are pointers by name. Backup tools handle each differently.

question: Compare nano and vi text editors for Linux.
correct_answer: NANO: Simple, beginner-friendly. All commands shown at bottom of screen. Uses Ctrl+key combinations. No modes — start typing immediately. Features: syntax highlighting (with -Y), line numbers, auto-indent. Easier to learn. Default editor in many distros for beginners. VI: Complex, powerful, universal. Three modes (command, insert, ex). Minimal interface — no menus/hints. Modes take time to learn but enable efficient editing. Ubiquitous (found on every Unix/Linux system). Features: powerful search/replace with regex, macros, registers, split windows, plugin support (vim). CHOOSE: nano for quick edits, vi/vim for serious work or on embedded/servers where only vi is available.
distractors: nano is available on every Linux system by default
vi cannot highlight syntax
nano supports macros and registers like vi does
explanation: vi is the only editor guaranteed to be on every Unix/Linux system (POSIX requirement). vim is the modern improved version.

question: Compare RPM and DEB package management systems in Linux.
correct_answer: RPM (.rpm): Red Hat Package Manager. Used by: RHEL, Fedora, CentOS, Rocky, AlmaLinux, SUSE, openSUSE. Low-level: rpm (install: rpm -ivh, query: rpm -qa, verify: rpm -V). High-level: dnf (modern RHEL 8+), yum (legacy RHEL 7). Repo files: /etc/yum.repos.d/. DEB (.deb): Debian package. Used by: Debian, Ubuntu, Mint, Kali, Pop!_OS. Low-level: dpkg (install: dpkg -i, query: dpkg -l, verify: dpkg --verify). High-level: apt (or apt-get). Repo files: /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.d/. BOTH: handle dependencies, support repositories, verify package integrity, track installed files. Neither is inherently better — choose based on distribution.
distractors: RPM packages work on Debian systems
apt and dnf are the same program with different names
DEB packages are more secure than RPM packages
explanation: The package format is tied to the distribution. Converting between them (alien) is possible but not recommended.

question: Compare the ifconfig and ip commands for network configuration.
correct_answer: ifconfig (net-tools): Legacy tool, deprecated. View: ifconfig (or ifconfig -a for all interfaces). Set IP: ifconfig eth0 192.168.1.10 netmask 255.255.255.0. Enable/disable: ifconfig eth0 up/down. No routing features — requires separate 'route' command. No longer installed by default on many modern distros. ip (iproute2): Modern replacement, actively maintained. View: ip addr show. Set IP: ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0. Enable/disable: ip link set eth0 up/down. Routing: ip route show, ip route add. Unified tool replaces ifconfig + route + arp. THE TRANSITION: Learn both (ifconfig still common in older docs/scripts) but use ip for new work.
distractors: ifconfig and ip use the same syntax for setting IP addresses
The ip command cannot configure wireless interfaces
ifconfig is the recommended tool for new Linux installations
explanation: iproute2 (ip) has been the standard since early 2000s. net-tools (ifconfig) is in maintenance mode.

topic: su vs sudo for Root Access
question: Compare su and sudo for acquiring root privileges in Linux.
correct_answer: su (switch user): 'su -' opens a root shell. Requires root password. Gives full root access for entire session. No audit trail. Risk: root password must be shared if multiple admins need access. Legacy approach. sudo (superuser do): 'sudo command' runs single command as root. Requires USER's password (not root's). Configurable in /etc/sudoers — allow specific commands only. Full audit trail (logged in /var/log/secure). No need to share root password. Timeout (default 5 min) remembers authentication. Modern distributions (Ubuntu, Fedora) disable root password — sudo is the only way. RECOMMENDATION: Always use sudo over su for better security and accountability.
distractors: sudo requires the root password to run commands
su - is more secure than sudo because it requires the root password
sudo does not log commands that were run
explanation: Ubuntu locks the root account by default — 'sudo -i' or 'sudo -s' replaces 'su -' for root shell access.

prompt: Arrange the stages of the Linux boot process in the correct order.
correct_sequence: BIOS/UEFI firmware performs POST (Power-On Self-Test) and identifies boot device
Boot loader (GRUB2) loads from MBR/GPT and presents boot menu
Kernel is loaded into memory and decompressed (from /boot/vmlinuz)
Kernel initializes hardware, mounts initial RAM filesystem (initramfs/initrd)
Kernel hands off to systemd (PID 1) as the first userspace process
systemd activates target units (basic.target → multi-user.target → graphical.target)
systemd starts system services (sshd, NetworkManager, httpd, etc.)
Login prompt (text-mode console or display manager for GUI) is presented
explanation: The boot process transitions from firmware → bootloader → kernel → init system → services. Each stage relies on the previous one completing successfully.

prompt: Arrange the steps to create a new user account in Linux in the correct order.
correct_sequence: Plan: determine username, UID, group membership, home directory location
Create the account: sudo useradd -m -c 'Full Name' -u UID -G supplementary_groups username
Set password: sudo passwd username (prompts for password)
Verify account: id username, ls -la /home/username, grep username /etc/passwd
(Optional) Set password aging: sudo chage -M 90 -W 7 username
(Optional) Grant sudo access: sudo visudo, add 'username ALL=(ALL) ALL' or use wheel/ sudo group
explanation: useradd creates the account entry in /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group. The password must be set separately. Home directory requires -m flag.

prompt: Arrange what happens when a shell script is executed from the command line.
correct_sequence: Shell reads the shebang line (#!/bin/sh) to determine the interpreter
Shell spawns the interpreter (/bin/sh, /bin/bash, etc.) as a child process
Interpreter reads and parses the script line by line
Variables are assigned and expanded ($name → value)
Command substitution is performed ($(command) or `command`)
Commands are executed sequentially, with pipes/redirections set up as needed
Conditional/loop structures (if/for/while) control flow based on test results
Script completes with exit status (exit 0 = success, non-zero = error)
explanation: The shebang is critical — if missing or wrong, the script runs in the current shell which may cause unexpected behavior.

question: A user gets 'Permission denied' when trying to access a file they should be able to read. What do you check?
correct_answer: 1. CHECK FILE PERMISSIONS: 'ls -l filename' — verify read permission for user/group/other. 2. CHECK OWNERSHIP: 'ls -l filename' shows owner and group. Is the user the owner? Is the user in the file's group? 3. CHECK DIRECTORY PERMISSIONS: the user needs EXECUTE (x) on ALL parent directories to access the file. Check with 'ls -ld /parent/dir'. 4. CHECK PARENT DIRECTORIES: 'namei -l /path/to/file' shows permissions on each component. 5. CHECK ACLs: 'getfacl filename' if ACLs are in use. 6. CHECK FILE ATTRIBUTES: 'lsattr filename' — immutable attribute (chattr +i) prevents all access. 7. CHECK SELINUX: 'ls -Z filename' and 'getenforce' — SELinux may be blocking even if DAC permissions allow.
explanation: Permission denied is often caused by missing execute permission on a parent directory, not the file itself. The directory execute bit controls access to directory contents.

question: A Linux server cannot connect to the Internet. Walk through the troubleshooting steps.
correct_answer: 1. CHECK INTERFACE STATUS: 'ip addr show' or 'ifconfig' — verify interface exists, is up, and has an IP address. 2. CHECK PHYSICAL LINK: 'ethtool eth0' — look for 'Link detected: yes'. Also check cable/switch. 3. CHECK DEFAULT GATEWAY: 'ip route show' or 'route -n' — default route should point to a reachable gateway. 4. PING GATEWAY: 'ping -c 4 gateway-ip' — if fails, problem is local (cable, interface config, wrong gateway). 5. PING PUBLIC IP: 'ping -c 4 8.8.8.8' — if works but DNS fails, DNS config is wrong. If fails, routing/firewall issue. 6. CHECK DNS: 'cat /etc/resolv.conf' — valid nameserver? 'nslookup google.com' or 'dig google.com' — does name resolution work? 7. CHECK FIREWALL: 'sudo iptables -L -n' or 'sudo firewall-cmd --list-all' — rules blocking outbound? 8. CHECK LOGS: 'journalctl -n 50' for network-related errors.

question: When installing a package, you get a dependency error. What do you do?
correct_answer: 1. READ THE ERROR: 'dnf install pkg' or 'apt install pkg' usually shows exactly which dependencies are missing. 2. USE THE PACKAGE MANAGER: dnf/apt automatically resolve dependencies from configured repositories. Try 'dnf clean all' then reinstall. 3. CHECK REPOSITORIES: 'dnf repolist' or 'apt-cache policy' — are the required repos enabled? Enable with: dnf config-manager --set-enabled repo or edit /etc/apt/sources.list. 4. SEARCH FOR THE MISSING DEPENDENCY: 'dnf provides */missingfile' or 'apt-file search missingfile' — find which package provides it. 5. FORCE INSTALL (CAREFUL): rpm -ivh --nodeps pkg.rpm or dpkg -i --ignore-depends=pkg — this may leave the system in an inconsistent state. 6. FIX BROKEN PACKAGES: 'dnf check' or 'apt --fix-broken install' — attempts to repair dependency issues. 7. CHECK FOR HELD/BLOCKED PACKAGES: 'dnf held' or 'apt-mark showhold' — held packages won't be updated.
explanation: Dependencies are packages your software needs to function. Always try to resolve through repositories first. Forcing installation without dependencies is risky.

What is Ternary Content-Addressable Memory (TCAM)?
answer: A specialized high-speed memory used in Cisco switches to store FIB entries for hardware forwarding. 'Ternary' means each bit can store 0, 1, or * (don't care). TCAM entries are compared in parallel (single clock cycle) enabling wire-speed forwarding decisions. Typically stores security ACLs and QoS ACLs in addition to routing entries.

question: What are Switch Database Management (SDM) templates?
answer: Predefined resource allocation profiles that partition TCAM space on Catalyst switches. Templates optimize for different network roles: (1) Default: balanced, (2) Access: maximizes ACL entries, (3) Routing: maximizes IPv4/IPv6 route entries, (4) VLAN: maximizes VLANs, (5) Dual IPv4/IPv6: balances between address families. Applied via `sdm prefer` command (requires reload).

question: What is process switching and how does it differ from CEF?
answer: The slowest forwarding mechanism where each packet is processed by the CPU. The router receives a packet, checks routing table, determines outgoing interface, rewrites MAC header, and forwards. The route is not cached, so every packet hits the CPU. CEF pre-builds FIB and adjacency tables, enabling hardware-based forwarding at much higher speeds.

question: What is the difference between centralized and distributed forwarding?
answer: Centralized forwarding: a single forwarding engine (usually the supervisor module) processes all packets. Distributed forwarding: line cards have their own forwarding ASICs with local copies of FIB/adjacency tables, forwarding traffic locally without involving the supervisor. Distributed forwarding provides higher throughput and is common on modular chassis switches.

question: What are the 802.1D STP port states and their progression?
answer: 1. BLOCKING: receives only BPDUs, no MAC learning, no forwarding (~20 sec Max Age). 2. LISTENING: sends/receives BPDUs, no MAC learning, no forwarding (15 sec Forward Delay). 3. LEARNING: sends/receives BPDUs, builds MAC table, no forwarding (15 sec Forward Delay). 4. FORWARDING: full operation. 5. DISABLED: administratively down. Total convergence: ~50 seconds (Max Age 20s + Forward Delay 15s + Forward Delay 15s).

question: What are the RSTP (802.1w) port roles?
answer: RSTP defines 5 port roles: (1) ROOT: the port that receives best BPDUs toward the root bridge. (2) DESIGNATED: the port on a segment that sends best BPDUs. (3) ALTERNATE: backup path to root (replaces blocking port, transitions immediately). (4) BACKUP: backup to designated port in shared-media segments. (5) DISABLED: administratively down. RSTP removes blocking/listening states — discarding replaces blocking.

question: How does RSTP achieve faster convergence than 802.1D?
answer: RSTP converges in ~1-3 seconds: (1) Uses explicit handshake (proposal/agreement) instead of timer-based convergence. (2) Edge ports (PortFast) transition immediately to forwarding. (3) Alternate ports instantly replace root ports on failure. (4) No distinction between blocking and listening (both are discarding). (5) BPDU timer: every 2 seconds (hello), 3 missed hellos = failure detection. RSTP changes are signaled — no topology change timers needed.

question: What is BPDU Guard and how does it work?
answer: A STP protection feature that disables a port if it receives any BPDU. Configured via `spanning-tree bpduguard enable` on the interface or globally with `spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default`. When a BPDU is received, the port goes into err-disabled state. Best practice: enable on all access ports to prevent unauthorized switch connections (STP manipulation attacks).

question: What is Root Guard?
answer: A STP protection feature that prevents an interface from becoming a root port. If the interface receives a superior BPDU (suggesting it should become root port), the port moves into root-inconsistent (blocking) state. Configured via `spanning-tree guard root`. Root Guard is enabled on interfaces expected to be designated ports — it ensures the current root bridge is not usurped by a rogue switch.

question: What is Loop Guard?
answer: A STP protection feature that prevents alternate/root ports from transitioning to designated forwarding when BPDUs stop arriving (unidirectional link failure). Without Loop Guard, a port that stops receiving BPDUs transitions to forwarding, creating a loop. Configured via `spanning-tree guard loop` or globally with `spanning-tree loopguard default`. Works with both 802.1D and RSTP.

question: What is Unidirectional Link Detection (UDLD)?
answer: A Cisco Layer 2 protocol that detects unidirectional links (fiber/SFP issues where traffic flows one way only). UDLD sends echo frames and expects acknowledgments. Modes: (1) NORMAL: detects and logs, takes action if bidirectional, (2) AGGRESSIVE: if echo not acknowledged for 8 seconds, attempts to re-establish, then err-disables the port. Works with STP Loop Guard to prevent bridging loops.

question: What is PortFast and when should it be used?
answer: A STP optimization that transitions a switch port directly to forwarding state, skipping blocking and learning. Configured via `spanning-tree portfast` on the interface. Use only on access ports connected to end hosts (routers, servers, PCs). NEVER use on trunk links or ports connecting to other switches. Must be used with BPDU Guard as safety measure to prevent accidental loops.

question: What is BPDU Filter and how does it differ from BPDU Guard?
answer: BPDU Filter prevents the switch from sending OR receiving BPDUs on a port. Config modes: (1) Per-interface (`spanning-tree bpdufilter enable`): blocks BPDUs completely. (2) Global with PortFast (`spanning-tree portfast bpdufilter default`): enables filtering only on PortFast-enabled ports. If a BPDU is received despite filter, the filter is removed and port reverts to normal STP. Risk: disabling BPDUs can create loops. Prefer BPDU Guard for security.

question: What is Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol (802.1s)?
answer: MSTP maps multiple VLANs to fewer spanning tree instances (MSTIs), reducing CPU/memory overhead. All VLANs within an MSTI share the same topology. MSTP is backward compatible with 802.1D RSTP and 802.1D STP. Key regions: MST region (group of switches with same name, revision, and VLAN mapping) uses multiple instances; outside the region, it presents as a single RSTP bridge per region.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch4: Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol
question: What is the difference between IST and MSTI in MSTP?
answer: IST (Internal Spanning Tree, Instance 0): mandatory spanning tree instance that includes all VLANs not explicitly mapped to other instances. IST represents the entire MST region to the outside world. MSTI (Multiple Spanning Tree Instance, 1-4094): optional instances created by mapping specific VLANs. Each MSTI runs RSTP internally within the MST region. Only IST carries BPDUs — MSTI information is encoded in IST BPDUs using M-record.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch4: Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol
question: What commands configure MST on Cisco switches?
answer: 1. `spanning-tree mode mst`: enables MST mode globally. 2. `spanning-tree mst configuration`: enters MST config mode. 3. `name NAME`: sets region name (must match all switches in region). 4. `revision N`: sets revision number. 5. `instance N vlan RANGE`: maps VLANs to MSTI. 6. `spanning-tree mst N priority VALUE`: sets root bridge priority for an MSTI. Verification: `show spanning-tree mst`.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch4: Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol
question: What defines an MST region?
answer: An MST region is a group of adjacent switches sharing three identical values: (1) region NAME (case-sensitive, up to 32 chars), (2) REVISION number (default 0), (3) VLAN-to-instance MAPPING. If any of these differ between switches, they are considered different regions and interact via RSTP. Each MST region appears as a single virtual bridge to the outside (CST/Common Spanning Tree).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch5: VLAN Trunks and EtherChannel Bundles
question: What is VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP)?
answer: A Cisco proprietary protocol that distributes VLAN configuration information across trunk links. VTP modes: (1) SERVER: creates/modifies/deletes VLANs, advertises changes (default), (2) CLIENT: receives and applies VLAN info, cannot modify, (3) TRANSPARENT: forwards VTP advertisements but does not participate, maintains local VLAN DB. Uses VTP revision number to determine latest update — higher revision wins. VTPv3 supports extended VLANs and private VLANs.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch5: VLAN Trunks and EtherChannel Bundles
question: What is Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP)?
answer: A Cisco proprietary protocol that automatically negotiates trunking between switch ports. DTP modes: (1) DYNAMIC AUTO: waits for peer to request trunk (passive). (2) DYNAMIC DESIRABLE: actively asks peer to become trunk (default on some platforms). (3) TRUNK: enables trunking unconditionally. (4) ACCESS: disables trunking. Security best practice: set ports to `switchport mode access` and disable DTP with `switchport nonegotiate` to prevent trunk negotiation attacks.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch5: VLAN Trunks and EtherChannel Bundles
question: What are LACP port modes?
answer: LACP (802.3ad) modes: (1) ACTIVE: sends LACP frames to negotiate etherchannel (initiates). (2) PASSIVE: responds to LACP frames but does not initiate. At least one side must be active. (3) ON: forces etherchannel without negotiation (not LACP). LACP provides: standardized negotiation, dynamic member addition/removal, misconfiguration detection, and hot-standby links. Configuration: `channel-group N mode active|passive` + `interface port-channel N`.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch5: VLAN Trunks and EtherChannel Bundles
question: What are PAgP port modes?
answer: PAgP (Port Aggregation Protocol) is Cisco proprietary. Modes: (1) DESIRABLE: initiates negotiation. (2) AUTO: responds passively. (3) ON: forces etherchannel without PAgP. Both desirable and auto can form if one side initiates. PAgP supports additional features: PAgP learning (silent/non-silent), PAgP secure (MAC-based authentication). Replaced by LACP in standards-based networks.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch5: VLAN Trunks and EtherChannel Bundles
question: How does EtherChannel load balancing work?
answer: EtherChannel load-balances frames across member links using a hash algorithm (not round-robin). Hash inputs (configurable via `port-channel load-balance METHOD`): src-ip, dst-ip, src-dst-ip, src-mac, dst-mac, src-dst-mac, src-port, dst-port, src-dst-port. The hash is computed on the first 6 to 8 bits of the selected fields, then modulo the number of active links determines the member port. Adding/removing links may rehash flows.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch5: VLAN Trunks and EtherChannel Bundles
question: What is LACP Fast (rate fast)?
answer: LACP Fast reduces the lacp rate from 30s (normal) to 1s. Configured via `lacp rate fast` on the interface. Enables faster detection of link failures (3 fast packets = 3s detection vs 90s normal). Best practice on all LACP bundles when supported by peers. Also configurable with `lacp min-bundle N` to ensure minimum active links before bundle activates.

question: What is Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF)?
answer: VRF allows multiple independent routing table instances on a single router. Each VRF has its own: RIB (Routing Information Base), FIB, routing protocol instances, and interface associations. Configured via: (1) `vrf definition NAME`, (2) `address-family ipv4`, (3) `interface GIX/Y: ip vrf forwarding NAME`.
