correct_answer: To avoid the split-horizon problem: with several PVCs on one physical interface, a routing protocol won't advertise routes learned on one PVC back out another — because split horizon forbids advertising out the same interface it learned on. Point-to-point subinterfaces (one DLCI each) make each PVC a separate logical interface, so the rule no longer applies.
distractors: Subinterfaces increase the CIR available on each PVC
Subinterfaces allow multiple IP networks on a single /30
Point-to-point subinterfaces automatically negotiate LMI types
Subinterfaces remove the need for frame-relay map statements
explanation: A point-to-point subinterface can have only one active DLCI; a multipoint subinterface can have many (and behaves like the physical interface). Wrong type = config must be removed, saved, and the router rebooted.

topic: Pinging Your Own Frame Relay Interface
question: Why does 'ping' to your own Frame Relay interface IP address fail, unlike on Ethernet?
correct_answer: Frame Relay interfaces have no predefined Layer-2 address — all Layer-2 addresses are configured manually. There is no DLCI for 'self'. To ping yourself you must map your own IP to a remote router's DLCI; the packet goes to the far router and comes back (RTT = 2x the PVC round trip). If that remote router fails, the self-ping fails too.
distractors: Ping to your own interface always works because the router owns the address
Frame Relay routers respond to pings from a virtual loopback DLCI
Self-ping fails because Frame Relay has no IP addressing at all
Ping to your own interface returns from the Frame Relay switch directly
explanation: A classic troubleshooting trap: Ethernet has permanent MACs; Frame Relay doesn't. Self-ping only works through a mapped remote router — and the ping time reflects the PVC round trip, not local processing.

question: In 'show frame-relay pvc' output, what does each PVC status mean?
correct_answer: Active = PVC up end to end and functioning. Inactive = the telecom switch knows the PVC, but you have no active mapping for it (forgot to map it). Deleted = you have a mapping, but the PVC it maps to doesn't exist (bad mapping). Static = no keepalive is configured on the interface.
distractors: Inactive means the telco hasn't provisioned the PVC yet
Deleted means the PVC is down because of an LMI type mismatch
Static means the PVC is permanently active and cannot be removed
Active means the PVC is provisioned on the switch but not mapped
explanation: The four statuses: Active (up end-to-end), Inactive (defined at switch, no working local mapping), Deleted (mapped but PVC doesn't exist), Static (no keepalives). LMI reports local-side information.

prompt: Arrange the steps to bring up a basic Frame Relay point-to-point link.
correct_sequence: 1. Configure Frame Relay encapsulation on the serial interface (encapsulation frame-relay)
2. Verify LMI status messages arrive (LMI counters increment, DTE LMI up)
3. Assign IP addresses to the interfaces
4. Let the router determine the far side automatically (point-to-point /30) or use Inverse ARP
5. For multi-node networks, add static mappings: frame-relay map ip <remote> <dlci> broadcast
6. Split PVCs into point-to-point subinterfaces if routing protocols are used
7. Verify with show frame-relay pvc and show frame-relay map
explanation: Encapsulation first (cisco default, ietf for non-Cisco), then LMI up, then IPs and mappings. Missing 'broadcast' on map statements breaks routing protocols. Each point-to-point subinterface needs its own /30.

prompt: Arrange the Frame Relay troubleshooting sequence.
correct_sequence: 1. Check the physical layer: cable plugged in, known-good cable, both ends connected
2. Verify the serial link is up (show interface — not administratively down)
3. Verify LMI is being received (LMI counters increment every 10 seconds)
4. Check the PVC status (show frame-relay pvc — Active/Inactive/Deleted)
5. Confirm the PVC is mapped to an interface (show frame-relay map)
6. Isolate the faulty side using local and remote debug frame-relay lmi output
7. Escalate to the provider if the switch reports the PVC as provisioned and active
explanation: Physical first, then LMI, then PVC status, then mappings. LMI status 0x2 = configured and active; 0x0 = configured but not active (usually your fault); missing entirely = telco hasn't provisioned it.

topic: Routing Protocol Not Forming Adjacency over Frame Relay
symptoms: The Frame Relay link is up and pings to the remote router succeed, but EIGRP or OSPF never establishes an adjacency between the two routers.
scenario_output:
show interface — Serial up, LMI DTE up, LMI counters incrementing
ping <remote> — succeeds
show frame-relay map — entry present: ip <remote> dlci 102, dynamic (no 'broadcast' listed)
correct_root_cause: The DLCI-to-IP mapping is missing the 'broadcast' keyword (or was learned via Inverse ARP, which does not carry broadcasts/multicasts). Routing protocol hellos/updates are multicast or broadcast, so they never cross the PVC.
recommended_fix: Replace the dynamic map with a static map including broadcast: 'frame-relay map ip <remote-ip> <dlci> broadcast'. Alternatively add 'frame-relay map ... broadcast' for each PVC.
explanation: Without 'broadcast' on the map statement, broadcasts, multicasts, and unicasts aren't carried over the PVC — killing routing protocol adjacencies even though unicast pings work.

prompt: Enter the command: encapsulation frame-relay
cloze_command: Router(config-if)# encapsulation frame-relay
explanation: Turns on Frame Relay on the serial interface. Default type is cisco; use 'encapsulation frame-relay ietf' when connecting to non-Cisco devices.

prompt: Enter the command: interface Serial0/0.102 point-to-point
cloze_command: Router(config)# interface Serial0/0.102 point-to-point
explanation: Creates a point-to-point subinterface (one DLCI). Then use 'frame-relay interface-dlci 102' to bind the DLCI. Point-to-point subinterfaces eliminate split-horizon issues.

question: Which buses make up the 6500-series switch backplane?
correct_answer: Four buses: the D bus (data bus, 32 Gbps, shared — all modules receive all frames), the R bus (results bus, 4 Gbps, module-to-supervisor switching logic), the C bus (control bus / EOBC, a 100 Mbps half-duplex network for management traffic and code downloads), and the crossbar fabric bus (up to 720 Gbps with a Supervisor-720).
distractors: Three buses: data, control, and management — all running at 32 Gbps
Two buses: the 32 Gbps data bus and the 720 Gbps fabric bus only
A single shared bus of 720 Gbps plus a separate power bus
The 6500 uses only the 6000-series 32 Gbps bus with no other options
explanation: The D bus behaves like a hub (broadcast to all); the crossbar fabric is a switch — modules communicate concurrently. The SFM provides the fabric; the Supervisor-720 integrates it.

question: What are the roles of the supervisor, the MSFC, and the PFC on a 6500?
correct_answer: The supervisor provides Layer-2 processing and is the chassis processor. The MSFC (multilayer switch feature card) is a daughter card that adds Layer-3 and higher routing functionality. The PFC (policy feature card) is a daughter card that performs QoS functions in hardware — no direct configuration needed. MSFC2/PFC2 pair with Sup-2; MSFC3/PFC3 are integral to the Sup-720.
distractors: The MSFC provides Layer-2 switching and the supervisor does routing
The PFC must be configured manually to enable QoS on each interface
The MSFC and PFC are only available on the Supervisor-1A
The supervisor handles all Layer-3 routing; the MSFC only caches ARP
explanation: Sup = L2 brain; MSFC = L3 routing engine; PFC = hardware QoS (and security/forwarding acceleration). Later supervisors include MSFC3 + PFC3 on-die.

question: Where must Supervisor-720 modules reside in a 6509 and a 6513 chassis, and why?
correct_answer: Because the Sup-720 includes the SFM (fabric) functionality, it must be placed in the SFM slots: slots 5 and 6 in a 6509, and slots 7 and 8 in a 6513. This frees slots 1/2 (6509) for line cards, unlike Sup-2 + separate SFMs which used 4 slots.
distractors: Sup-720s can go in any slot since the fabric is integrated
Sup-720s must always reside in slots 1 and 2 of every chassis
The Sup-720 is only supported in the 6513 chassis
Sup-720s use slots 3 and 4 to keep line cards in the first slots
explanation: A redundant 6509 with Sup-2s needs slots 1/2 for supervisors plus 5/6 for SFMs — leaving five line-card slots. Sup-720s in 5/6 free slots 1/2 — a major slot-density win.

question: What happens when a nonfabric-enabled module (like an older CSM) is installed in a 6500 with fabric-only modules and a Supervisor-720?
correct_answer: The whole switch downgrades to a slower operating mode: the supervisor reverts to bus/truncated mode instead of dCEF, and the 720 Gbps fabric capability is lost — one nonfabric blade holds the entire chassis back. Fabric-only modules have a single connector to the fabric (no D-bus); fabric-enabled modules have both.
distractors: The nonfabric module is automatically upgraded to fabric status
Only the traffic crossing the nonfabric module is slowed down
The fabric continues at 720 Gbps and the CSM is bypassed
The supervisor powers down the nonfabric module entirely
explanation: show fabric switching-mode reveals 'Truncated' mode and 'Bus' entries when a nonfabric blade (e.g., CSM) is present. The lesson: understand how your modules interoperate before mixing them.

question: What is Virtual Switching System (VSS) on the 6500?
correct_answer: VSS clusters two 6500s into a single logical switch (like 3750 stacking at chassis scale). It requires redundant supervisors in SSO mode, a matching 'switch virtual domain', virtual MACs, and a Virtual Switch Link (VSL) — a resilient EtherChannel, ideally with links distributed across modules and in powers of two. The VSL port-channel number must DIFFER on each switch.
distractors: VSS requires identical VSL port-channel numbers on both switches
VSS uses the management ports as the virtual switch link
VSS is a load-balancing protocol between two independent switches
VSS can cluster up to nine 6500 chassis in one logical switch
explanation: After 'switch convert mode virtual', interfaces are renamed to switch/slot/port. Only the active chassis accepts configuration; the standby prompt shows '-sdby'. VSS enables split EtherChannels across chassis (MEC).

question: How does failover work in a VSS cluster, and what are the reload caveats?
correct_answer: The active role transfers only when the active chassis reloads; the standby supervisor takes over active duties in under one second. 'reload' on the active chassis reloads the ENTIRE cluster. Use 'redundancy reload peer' to reboot only the standby, 'redundancy reload shelf' to reload one chassis, or 'redundancy force-switchover' to force failover (which reloads the active).
distractors: Failover is hitless and requires no reload of the active chassis
The standby automatically takes over when the active is overloaded
'reload' on the active switch reboots only that chassis
VSS failover can be forced without reloading any chassis
explanation: VSS does not fail over like firewalls — the active must reload. A full chassis reload can take up to 15 minutes; the standby supervisor's takeover itself is under a second.

question: What is a dual-active (split-brain) scenario in VSS, and how is it detected?
correct_answer: Dual-active = both physical switches become active and both own the same IP addresses. Detection methods: enhanced PAgP messages (recommended for all-Cisco environments — requires trust mode on the connecting port channel), BFD, and fast-hello. All three are enabled by default on the VSS pair.
distractors: Dual-active is prevented by keeping both switches in the same rack
Enhanced PAgP detection requires an IOS version from 1998 or earlier
Dual-active detection uses the VSL link's keepalive only
The standby switch never becomes active without a full reboot
explanation: Split-brain is dangerous (duplicate IPs). Enhanced PAgP signals the problem when a third switch is connected to the cluster; 'dual-active detection pagp trust channel-group X' configures the trusted MEC.

question: What makes the FWSM (Firewall Services Module) different from a firewall appliance in the 6500?
correct_answer: Its interfaces are switched virtual interfaces (SVIs) tied to VLANs, not physical ports — there can be hundreds of them. It supports multiple contexts (virtual firewalls for different customers/functions) and exceeds 5 Gbps of throughput by communicating over the backplane instead of Ethernet cables. Access it from IOS with 'session slot <x> proc 1'; in multi-context mode use 'changeto context'.
distractors: The FWSM is limited to two physical firewall interfaces
The FWSM runs CatOS and cannot be configured with PIX commands
The FWSM requires an external management station for all configuration
The FWSM supports only a single security context
explanation: FWSM = the last PIX-lineage product, now a module. Because it talks over the backplane it beat the top PIX appliance (1.7 Gbps) with 5+ Gbps. Contexts enable per-customer virtual firewalls.

question: What is the Network Analysis Module (NAM) on the 6500?
correct_answer: Essentially an RMON probe and packet-capture device in a blade. It captures packets like an external analyzer (via web interface), can run multiple capture sessions, and can analyze traffic anywhere on the network using RSPAN sources — invaluable during outages.
distractors: The NAM is a load-balancing module for web server farms
The NAM is an IPS that blocks attacks in real time
The NAM only monitors the supervisor's own control traffic
The NAM requires a separate external Linux server to run
explanation: NAM = RMON + packet capture + RSPAN monitoring from a single blade. Web-based interface; no extra software. Limited smart alarm indications compared with high-end analyzers.

question: What was the Content Switching Module (CSM), and what limitation did it have?
correct_answer: The CSM was Cisco's load-balancing module for the 6500 (4 Gbps, optional SSL accelerator daughter card). Its big drawback: it is NOT fabric-enabled — it's a 32 Gbps blade, so installing one makes the supervisor revert to bus mode and kills dCEF/720 Gbps operation. It has been replaced by the fabric-enabled ACE module.
distractors: The CSM is fabric-only and requires a Supervisor-720 to work
The CSM replaced the ACE module in the 6500
The CSM supports stateful failover only with ACE modules
The CSM's 32 Gbps connection speeds up the entire chassis
explanation: CSMs sync configs for stateful failover (v4.2(1)+). The lesson: an expensive blade can bottleneck the whole switch — the CSM's nonfabric backplane connection forces bus mode.

prompt: Arrange the steps to convert a pair of standalone 6509s into a VSS cluster.
correct_sequence: 1. Configure redundancy mode SSO on each switch (redundancy → mode sso)
2. Define the matching virtual switch domain (switch virtual domain 100)
3. Assign switch numbers (switch 1 on the left, switch 2 on the right)
4. Use virtual MAC addresses (mac-address use-virtual)
5. Build the VSL: create a port channel on each switch (switch virtual link <n>)
6. Add physical ports to the channel with 'channel-group X mode on' (no negotiation)
7. Run 'switch convert mode virtual' on each switch — interfaces renumber to switch/slot/port
explanation: The VSL port-channel number must differ per switch (Po10 vs Po20) so the pair can distinguish sides after merging. Conversion saves config and reloads. VSL links should be high-speed, across modules, in powers of two.

symptoms: A 6509 with Supervisor-720s and fabric-only Ethernet modules performs far below the expected 720 Gbps. Throughput bottlenecks appear during peak traffic, and load-balanced traffic suffers.
scenario_output:
show fabric switching-mode — Global switching mode is Truncated; some modules show 'Bus'
show module — one WS-X6066 (CSM) or other nonfabric module present
correct_root_cause: A nonfabric-enabled module (e.g., an older CSM) is installed in the chassis. Any nonfabric blade forces the supervisor to revert from dCEF to a slower bus/truncated mode, so the whole switch loses the 720 Gbps fabric speed.
recommended_fix: Remove or replace the nonfabric module with a fabric-enabled equivalent (e.g., replace the CSM with an ACE module), then verify 'show fabric switching-mode' shows Crossbar/dCEF for all modules.
explanation: The supervisor must compromise to let nonfabric modules participate, degrading the entire chassis. Check module fabric class before mixing blades in a fabric-based design.

prompt: Enter the command: switch virtual domain 100
cloze_command: Router(config)# switch virtual domain 100
explanation: Defines the VSS domain (1-255); must match on both switches. Only takes effect after 'switch convert mode virtual' is issued.
